meta.blurb: Frederick Douglass never knew his birthday, and he was told that learning to read would spoil him as a slave. He learned anyway. This is his own account, naming real people and places, of how he fought back and got free.
meta.bible: Frederick Douglass: born Frederick Bailey into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland, about 1817 or 1818; the author of the Narrative, 1845; died in 1895. Harriet Bailey: his mother, who walked twelve miles at night to see him; she died when he was about seven. Betsy Bailey: his grandmother. Colonel Lloyd: the rich planter whose estate was the Great House Farm. Captain Anthony: Colonel Lloyd's manager and Frederick's first owner. Aunt Hester: Frederick's aunt, beaten by Captain Anthony. Mr Gore: a cruel overseer who shot Demby. Mr Severe: an overseer. Mr Hopkins: an overseer. Demby: an enslaved man shot by Mr Gore. Lucretia Auld: Captain Anthony's daughter, who was kind to Frederick. Thomas Auld: her husband and later Frederick's owner at St Michaels; mean and fond of religion. Hugh Auld: Thomas's brother, who lived in Baltimore. Sophia Auld: Hugh's wife, who first taught Frederick the alphabet. Edward Covey: the farmer known as a breaker of slaves, 1833. William Freeland: a fairer farmer who hired Frederick in 1834. Sandy Jenkins: an enslaved man with a free wife, who gave Frederick a root. David Ruggles: a Black abolitionist in New York. Anna Murray: a free woman of Baltimore who became Frederick's wife. Nathan Johnson: his host in New Bedford, who suggested the name Douglass. William Lloyd Garrison: the editor of The Liberator and the writer of the preface. Wendell Phillips: a campaigner who wrote a letter for the book. Abraham Lincoln: the President. Maryland. Baltimore. Wye. Easton. St Michaels. Chesapeake Bay. Georgia. New York. New Bedford. Massachusetts. Nantucket. Lynn. Ireland. Britain. Washington. Great House Farm. The Columbian Orator: a schoolbook of speeches. The Liberator: an antislavery newspaper. The North Star: Douglass's newspaper, 1847. The Lady of the Lake: a poem by Sir Walter Scott. Methodist. Christianity. Bible. Tuckahoe. Civil War. Black. Easter. Christmas. Georgia. Voice and tone: serious, dignified and clear; truthful and never graphic; cruelty is stated plainly and briefly with no gore; the writer admires Douglass's courage. Added for the full-length book: Sally Lloyd: the sloop that carried Frederick to Baltimore, under Captain Edward Dodson. Fell's Point: the Baltimore shipbuilding district where Hugh Auld lived. Aunt Katy: Captain Anthony's cruel cook. Andrew Anthony: Captain Anthony's son. Rowena Hamilton: Thomas Auld's second wife. William Hamilton: a farmer near St Michaels. Henry Harris, John Harris, Henry Bailey, Charles Roberts: the men who planned the escape with Frederick. Hughes and Bill Smith: workers on Covey's farm. Mr Gardner: a Baltimore shipbuilder. Esquire Watson: a Baltimore magistrate. Walter Price: a Baltimore shipbuilder. Mary Johnson: Nathan Johnson's wife. Mary: Hamilton's enslaved girl. Henrietta: Hamilton's enslaved girl. Mrs Hamilton: a Baltimore neighbour who ill-treated two enslaved girls. Sheridan: the speaker whose speeches Frederick read. Rochester: the New York city where The North Star began. Seneca Falls: the New York town of the 1848 women's rights convention. Dublin: the Irish city where an edition of the Narrative appeared. Cambria. Pennington: James W C Pennington, the minister who married Frederick and Anna. Easton: the Maryland town with the jail. Hillsborough. Alabama. Newport. Boston. Patrick Henry: a Revolutionary speaker. Phillips. Lion. Luke. Eastern Shore. Mexican. Vigilance Committee. District of Columbia. Catholic. Irish. Americans. Britain. Fell. Hamilton. Hugh. Sophia. Garrison. Seneca. Haiti. Ellen Richardson: a British friend who helped buy his freedom. Richardson. Webster. Biblical. Sunday. Saturday. Monday. Friday. February. August. September. April. July. March.

beats.scene: An editor in a dark coat sits at a desk with a printed page
beats.summary: Garrison's preface recalls the antislavery meeting on Nantucket in August 1841, where he first heard Douglass.

beats.scene: A young man rises nervously from a seat in a crowded meeting hall
beats.summary: Douglass, a stranger, is urged to speak and comes forward with embarrassment.

beats.scene: A hushed audience listens to a speaker standing on a low platform
beats.summary: Douglass tells his life under slavery, and Garrison's hatred of slavery has never been stronger.

beats.scene: A white-haired editor points toward a young speaker as the crowd calls out
beats.summary: Garrison compares the speech to Patrick Henry's and asks whether they heard a thing or a man.

beats.scene: A speaker addresses townspeople in a wooden hall under oil lamps
beats.summary: The Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society hires Douglass, and many doubt that so fine a speaker was ever a slave.

beats.scene: A neat title page lies open on a table beside an inkwell
beats.summary: Douglass writes the book himself and names real people, places and dates, which is risky for a fugitive.

beats.scene: A folded letter and a pair of spectacles rest on a desk
beats.summary: Garrison vouches that the book is true in every statement, exaggerates nothing and falls short of the reality.

beats.scene: A man writes a letter by lamplight while a stone lion looks on
beats.summary: Wendell Phillips opens his letter with the fable of the man and the lion.

beats.scene: A hand holds a quill above a blank page in a quiet study
beats.summary: Phillips is glad that the lions now write history, as slavery had been described by others.

beats.scene: A tall wooden door stands open onto a bright field
beats.summary: Phillips says the book shows slavery from the inside, and Douglass begins his story.

beats.scene: A flat Maryland farm with a small cabin under a wide sky
beats.summary: Douglass opens by saying he was born in Tuckahoe, Talbot County, Maryland, near Hillsborough.

beats.scene: Field workers rest at midday beneath a spring sun and a cherry tree
beats.summary: Enslaved people kept time by planting time, harvest time and cherry time, not by dates.

beats.scene: A small boy watches white children celebrate on a sunny porch
beats.summary: White children knew their ages; his master said a slave had no right to ask.

beats.scene: A boy gazes across a field toward a distant white house
beats.summary: His father was a white man, rumoured to be his master, and he never learned the truth.

beats.scene: A heavy law book lies open on a table in a courthouse
beats.summary: The law made a child follow the condition of its mother, so slaveholders profited from their own children.

beats.scene: A mother kisses a baby, then hands him to an old woman
beats.summary: Before he was a year old, Frederick was parted from his mother, as was the custom.

beats.scene: A tired woman walks alone along a dark country road beneath stars
beats.summary: Harriet Bailey, hired out twelve miles away, walked the road at night after her day's work.

beats.scene: A woman lies beside a sleeping boy in a dim cabin
beats.summary: He saw his mother only four or five times, always at night, and she left before dawn.

beats.scene: A woman holds an open book while a small boy watches her
beats.summary: Harriet could read, the only one in Tuckahoe, and Douglass thinks his love of learning came from her.

beats.scene: A small boy stands apart from a few mourners at a graveside
beats.summary: His mother died when he was about seven; he was not allowed to be with her.

beats.scene: An old woman mends a fishing net outside a small cabin
beats.summary: His grandmother Betsy Bailey was admired for her nets and her luck with sweet potatoes.

beats.scene: A small boy plays in the dirt outside a cabin door
beats.summary: Old women raised the children, and Frederick lived in her cabin until he was about six.

beats.scene: An old woman and a small boy walk along a long country road
beats.summary: His grandmother takes him on foot to Colonel Lloyd's plantation, where his master lives.

beats.scene: A boy meets a girl and a boy in a busy farmyard
beats.summary: He meets his brother and sisters, who are almost strangers to him.

beats.scene: A small boy lies face down on the ground, crying
beats.summary: His grandmother slips away while he plays, and he weeps bitterly.

beats.scene: A grand white house stands among fields beside a wide river
beats.summary: Colonel Lloyd's estate lies by the Wye River; Captain Anthony manages it for him.

beats.scene: A blacksmith, a weaver and a carpenter work in a busy yard
beats.summary: The estate is like a village with every trade, all worked by the enslaved.

beats.scene: Men with empty baskets walk along a sandy lane toward a great house
beats.summary: Men chosen from each farm fetch the monthly food allowance; it is an honour.

beats.scene: Men carrying baskets sing as they walk through a forest road
beats.summary: On the road they sing wild songs, a mix of joy and deep sadness.

beats.scene: An older man listens beside a quiet path as the singing fades
beats.summary: Douglass later understands the songs as protests and prayers, not signs of contentment.

beats.scene: A stern man in a long coat watches workers in a farmyard
beats.summary: Captain Anthony was not thought especially cruel, yet he sometimes whipped in a passion and seemed to take pleasure in it.

beats.scene: A young woman stands before a frowning man in a farm kitchen
beats.summary: Frederick's aunt Hester, forbidden to keep company with Ned Roberts, angers Captain Anthony.

beats.scene: A boy hides inside a dark cupboard as a woman cries out
beats.summary: Anthony whips Hester, and Frederick hides in a closet, terrified.

beats.scene: A boy stands alone in a doorway at first light
beats.summary: Douglass calls it the blood-stained gate, the entrance to the hell of slavery.

beats.scene: A sack of cornmeal and some salted fish rest on a shelf
beats.summary: The monthly food allowance and yearly clothing on Lloyd's estate were small.

beats.scene: A child in a thin shirt shivers outside on a frosty morning
beats.summary: Children received two coarse shirts a year and had no shoes, stockings or jackets.

beats.scene: A boy curls up inside a corn sack on a cold floor
beats.summary: No bed was given; the children had no blanket and Frederick's feet cracked with frost.

beats.scene: Children crowd around a long wooden trough in a muddy yard
beats.summary: Cornmeal porridge was poured into a trough and eaten like pig feed.

beats.scene: A stout cook scolds a hungry boy at a kitchen door
beats.summary: Aunt Katy, the cook, punished Frederick by keeping him from his food.

beats.scene: A small boy drives cows across a dusty farmyard at sunset
beats.summary: Too young for the fields, Frederick drove the cows, guarded the garden and ran errands.

beats.scene: A tall wooden fence beside a garden full of ripe fruit
beats.summary: Colonel Lloyd's garden held fruit of every kind, from the northern apple to the southern orange.

beats.scene: A man paints black tar along the boards of a high fence
beats.summary: To stop theft, the colonel had the whole fence tarred.

beats.scene: A man with a black stain on his sleeve faces an angry master
beats.summary: Any slave found with tar on him was whipped, guilty or not.

beats.scene: An old coachman stands bareheaded beside a pair of fine horses
beats.summary: Old Barney, the coachman, was blamed and whipped whatever he did, and could not answer back.

beats.scene: Two men meet on a dusty road in the afternoon sun
beats.summary: Colonel Lloyd, not knowing a slave by sight, asks him on the road about his master.

beats.scene: A man walks away from a farm beside a stranger with a wagon
beats.summary: The honest man is sold to a Georgia trader for finding fault with his master.

beats.scene: Two enslaved men speak quietly in a barn, glancing at the door
beats.summary: After such cases, slaves said that they were content and their masters kind.

beats.scene: Two enslaved men argue across a fence at the end of a workday
beats.summary: Slaves quarrelled over whose master was richest or kindest, a sign of how slavery twisted minds.

beats.scene: An overseer in a long coat curses as workers bend over their rows
beats.summary: Mr Severe was a hard, violent overseer, and his death seemed a mercy to the slaves.

beats.scene: A quiet overseer speaks softly to workers at the edge of a field
beats.summary: Mr Hopkins was quieter and whipped less, but he left quickly, and Mr Gore took his place.

beats.scene: A proud overseer in a tall hat rides slowly beside a field
beats.summary: Mr Gore was proud, ambitious and cruel, and allowed no slave to answer back.

beats.scene: A man stands neck-deep in a creek while an overseer watches
beats.summary: After a whipping, Demby runs into a creek and refuses to come out.

beats.scene: An overseer raises a gun toward a creek as workers watch
beats.summary: Gore calls three times, then shoots Demby dead.

beats.scene: Planters talk gravely around a table while an overseer stands aside
beats.summary: Gore says Demby set a dangerous example; no one calls him to account.

beats.scene: An empty judge's bench stands in a quiet courtroom
beats.summary: Killing a slave was hardly treated as a crime, as black witnesses were not heard.

beats.scene: A kind young woman hands bread and butter to a boy at a door
beats.summary: Lucretia Auld, Captain Anthony's daughter, was kind to Frederick.

beats.scene: A young woman talks gently to a boy beneath a large oak tree
beats.summary: At about eight, Frederick is chosen to go to Baltimore to live with Hugh Auld.

beats.scene: A boy scrubs himself in a shallow creek on a bright morning
beats.summary: Lucretia tells him to wash away the plantation dirt first, and he scrubs for three days.

beats.scene: A boy holds up a first pair of trousers, smiling
beats.summary: She promises him trousers, the first he has ever owned.

beats.scene: A small boy at the bow of a sailing sloop watches the shore
beats.summary: Frederick sails to Baltimore on the Sally Lloyd, feeling no regret; he later sees it as providence.

beats.scene: A sloop ties up at a crowded wharf with tall brick buildings behind
beats.summary: Frederick reaches Baltimore and is taken to Hugh Auld's house at Fell's Point.

beats.scene: A smiling woman greets a small boy at a brick doorway
beats.summary: Sophia Auld welcomes him with a kind face, and he is not used to such kindness.

beats.scene: A woman sits at a window sewing while a small boy plays beside her
beats.summary: Sophia had never owned a slave and had earned her own living, so she treated him gently.

beats.scene: A woman and a boy sit side by side with an open spelling book
beats.summary: Sophia teaches him the alphabet and then words of three or four letters.

beats.scene: A man frowns at a spelling book in a Baltimore sitting room
beats.summary: Hugh Auld finds out and forbids the lessons as unlawful and unsafe.

beats.scene: An angry man points at his wife while a boy listens at the door
beats.summary: Hugh says a slave should know only how to obey; give an inch and he takes a mile.

beats.scene: A stern man lectures a woman by lamplight in a quiet parlour
beats.summary: Learning would make a slave unmanageable, unfit, discontented and unhappy, says Hugh.

beats.scene: A boy sits very still on a stair, thinking hard
beats.summary: Frederick suddenly understands how white men keep Black people enslaved.

beats.scene: A boy opens a small book with a determined face
beats.summary: He sees that learning is the pathway to freedom and decides to learn at any cost.

beats.scene: A woman snatches a newspaper from a boy's hands in a kitchen
beats.summary: Sophia, now stern and watchful, snatches away his papers; slavery has hardened her.

beats.scene: A boy walks along a busy Baltimore street past brick houses and shops
beats.summary: A city slave is almost free compared with a plantation slave, partly from a sense of shame.

beats.scene: A thin girl sits on a cold doorstep beside a closed door
beats.summary: Near the Aulds, Mrs Hamilton ill-treats Henrietta and Mary, and neighbours report her.

beats.scene: A boy shares bread with hungry white boys on a street corner
beats.summary: Frederick has bread, the poor white boys do not; he trades bread for lessons.

beats.scene: A boy studies a small spelling book on a wharf between errands
beats.summary: He carries a spelling book on errands; he does not name his young teachers, to protect them.

beats.scene: A boy speaks earnestly to white boys on a street corner
beats.summary: He tells the boys they will be free at twenty-one while he is a slave for life.

beats.scene: A boy sits at a table by a window as the seasons change
beats.summary: He lives in Hugh Auld's family about seven years and learns to read and write.

beats.scene: A boy sits on a wooden crate reading a thick book beside a dock
beats.summary: At about twelve he gets hold of The Columbian Orator and reads it constantly.

beats.scene: A page shows two men in conversation, one seated and one standing
beats.summary: A dialogue between a master and a slave who ran away three times ends with the slave freed.

beats.scene: A boy reads aloud a speech in an empty room, book open
beats.summary: Sheridan's speeches on Catholic rights give voice to his own thoughts.

beats.scene: A boy stands by a harbour window, gazing at distant sails
beats.summary: The more he reads, the more he hates his enslavers, yet he sees no way out.

beats.scene: A boy sits alone at a window with a closed book on his knee
beats.summary: Reading feels like a curse as well as a blessing; he envies the ignorant and wishes he were a beast.

beats.scene: A boy hears angry men shouting on a Baltimore street corner
beats.summary: He keeps hearing the word abolition, spoken with anger, whenever a slave runs away.

beats.scene: A boy turns the pages of a large dictionary in a quiet corner
beats.summary: The dictionary explains abolition as the act of abolishing, but not what is to be abolished.

beats.scene: A boy reads a Baltimore newspaper beneath a street lamp
beats.summary: A newspaper reveals petitions to end slavery in the District of Columbia and the slave trade.

beats.scene: Two workmen unload a stone barge on a Baltimore dock, talking to a boy
beats.summary: Two Irish dockworkers tell Frederick to escape to the north, where he would be free.

beats.scene: A boy nods politely to two workmen while his eyes look worried
beats.summary: Fearing a trap for a reward, he hides his feelings, but the words stay with him.

beats.scene: A boy writes carefully on scrap paper at a small table
beats.summary: He resolves to learn to write so that he can write a pass for himself.

beats.scene: A boy studies chalk letters on wooden planks in a busy shipyard
beats.summary: Shipyard carpenters mark timbers with L, S, F and A; he learns the letters and copies them.

beats.scene: A boy chalks letters on a wooden fence while another boy watches
beats.summary: He challenges boys who can write; each shows him new letters, and walls and fences become his slate.

beats.scene: A boy copies from a schoolbook at a kitchen table in a quiet house
beats.summary: He copies Tommy Auld's old copybooks when the house is empty until his hand matches.

beats.scene: A boy reads a letter in a Baltimore kitchen, looking worried
beats.summary: Captain Anthony dies, leaving a son and a daughter, and Frederick is sent for to be valued.

beats.scene: Men, women and children stand in a line beside horses and cattle
beats.summary: At the valuation, people were ranked and examined like the farm animals.

beats.scene: A boy looks anxiously at a burly man while an older woman stands near
beats.summary: Frederick fears falling to Andrew Anthony, but he falls to Lucretia.

beats.scene: A sloop sails across a wide bay toward a distant city
beats.summary: Lucretia sends him back to Baltimore, and he is glad to return.

beats.scene: An old woman sits alone by a cold hearth in a small wooden hut
beats.summary: His grandmother, after a lifetime of service, is left alone in a hut in the woods.

beats.scene: An old woman stoops to place a log on a dying fire at night
beats.summary: She had nursed the master's family, yet no one came to comfort her.

beats.scene: A man writes by candlelight with a troubled face
beats.summary: Douglass asks whether a righteous God will not punish such things.

beats.scene: A few mourners gather around a wooden coffin in a country graveyard
beats.summary: Lucretia and Andrew die; the family is broken up and Thomas Auld remarries Rowena Hamilton.

beats.scene: Two brothers argue angrily in a doorway as a boy waits
beats.summary: Thomas Auld quarrels with Hugh and takes Frederick away from Baltimore.

beats.scene: A boy looks back from a boat at a brick city fading into mist
beats.summary: In March 1832 Frederick leaves Baltimore for St Michaels.

beats.scene: A lean boy looks through a window at a laden table
beats.summary: At St Michaels, Thomas Auld is a mean master who gives his slaves too little food.

beats.scene: A thin boy creeps toward a pantry shelf in the half dark
beats.summary: Frederick is so hungry that he sometimes takes food in secret.

beats.scene: A boy stands at a pantry door, thinking, a loaf in his hand
beats.summary: He argues that taking his master's food is not stealing, since he and the food are both his master's.

beats.scene: Tents and wagons stand among tall trees at a late summer meeting
beats.summary: In August 1832 Thomas Auld is converted at a Methodist camp meeting, and Frederick hopes for kindness.

beats.scene: A man kneels loudly in prayer at a family table while a servant waits
beats.summary: Auld prays morning and evening but grows crueller.

beats.scene: A man with a Bible stands over a bowed young woman
beats.summary: Auld whips a lame young woman and quotes Scripture to justify it.

beats.scene: A preacher and a master pray in a parlour; a servant waits
beats.summary: Douglass concludes that religious slaveholders are the worst of all.

beats.scene: Young men and women sit on benches in a crowded room
beats.summary: Frederick starts a Sunday school to teach other enslaved people to read.

beats.scene: Armed men with sticks burst into a small room full of startled students
beats.summary: Churchmen break up the school with sticks, a bitter irony.

beats.scene: A farmer shakes hands with a lean young man at a gate
beats.summary: Auld says the city spoiled Frederick and hires him for a year to Edward Covey.

beats.scene: A hard-faced farmer in a black coat stands before a small farmhouse
beats.summary: Edward Covey, a poor farm renter and church class leader, is famous for breaking young slaves.

beats.scene: A young man walks a country road toward a distant farmhouse
beats.summary: On 1 January 1833 Frederick goes to Covey's farm, about seven miles from St Michaels.

beats.scene: Wild oxen drag a cart through a gate in a spray of splinters
beats.summary: Frederick cannot control a team of wild oxen, the cart is wrecked, and Covey whips him.

beats.scene: A worker bends in a field while the sun rises behind him
beats.summary: Covey works them from first light to last, and for six months whips Frederick almost every week.

beats.scene: A man crawls on hands and knees through tall corn, peering between the stalks
beats.summary: Covey spies on his workers by creeping through the fields, and the slaves call him the snake.

beats.scene: A young man sits slumped against a fence, his face blank and tired
beats.summary: Frederick is broken in body, soul and spirit; his love of reading fades.

beats.scene: A young man stands on a high bank watching white sails
beats.summary: On Sundays he watches the ships on Chesapeake Bay, which seem like ghosts to him.

beats.scene: A young man speaks to distant ships with an outstretched arm
beats.summary: He speaks to the ships, saying they are free and he is a slave, and wishes he were aboard.

beats.scene: A young man sits on the ground, looking north with a resolute face
beats.summary: Frederick resolves to run away, since he has only one life to lose.

beats.scene: A farmer prays with his family at a table at dawn
beats.summary: Covey leads loud family prayers, yet his religion makes him no kinder to his workers.

beats.scene: A young man sways in a hot wheat yard as workers fan grain
beats.summary: In August 1833 Frederick, working in the heat, becomes dizzy and ill.

beats.scene: A young man lies on the ground while a farmer stands over him
beats.summary: Frederick collapses; Covey kicks him, then strikes him on the head, drawing blood.

beats.scene: A bleeding young man walks alone into a dark forest
beats.summary: He decides to appeal to Thomas Auld and walks seven miles through the woods.

beats.scene: A bloodied young man stands before his master in a doorway
beats.summary: Auld says Covey is a good man and that Frederick must go back, or he will lose the year's wages.

beats.scene: A young man hides among tall trees as a farmer searches with a whip
beats.summary: Covey chases him with a cowskin; Frederick runs into the woods and hides.

beats.scene: A hungry young man sits among trees as evening falls
beats.summary: Frederick is hungry and sore, and cannot go back or stay away.

beats.scene: Two men sit by a small fire near a cottage in a clearing
beats.summary: He meets Sandy Jenkins, an enslaved man with a free wife, who takes him in.

beats.scene: An older man hands a dry root to a young man
beats.summary: Sandy gives him a root to carry in his right pocket, saying no white man could whip him.

beats.scene: A young man walks back toward a farmhouse on a sunlit Sunday morning
beats.summary: On Sunday he meets Covey, dressed for church, who greets him kindly.

beats.scene: A farmer creeps into a dim stable with a rope
beats.summary: On Monday Covey comes into the stable with a rope and seizes Frederick's legs.

beats.scene: A young man grips a farmer by the throat in a dim stable
beats.summary: Frederick suddenly resolves to fight and seizes Covey by the throat.

beats.scene: A larger man trembles as a young man holds him by the collar
beats.summary: Covey is startled and trembles; Frederick says he will go on resisting, come what may.

beats.scene: Two hired workers stand apart as a farmer calls for help
beats.summary: Hughes is kicked away and Bill Smith refuses to help Covey.

beats.scene: Two figures grapple in a cloud of dust on the stable floor
beats.summary: They fight for nearly two hours until Covey lets go, puffing, though he never whipped him.

beats.scene: A young man works calmly in a field while a farmer watches from afar
beats.summary: For six more months Covey never touches him; he feared for his name as a breaker.

beats.scene: A young man stands tall, gazing at the horizon
beats.summary: Douglass calls the fight the turning point of his life as a slave.

beats.scene: A young man stands firmly in a field as an overseer says nothing
beats.summary: He resolves never again to be a slave in fact, whatever he remains in form.

beats.scene: A sunrise breaks over a field as a young man lifts his head
beats.summary: He describes a resurrection from the tomb of slavery; his spirit rises and defiance replaces fear.

beats.scene: A young man works in a field while a farmer passes without looking
beats.summary: He stays at Covey's until Christmas without being beaten again.

beats.scene: A dry root lies on a worn table beside a candle
beats.summary: Whether or not the root had power, Frederick knows that his own courage changed his life.

beats.scene: Enslaved men play ball and wrestle in a field during a holiday
beats.summary: Between Christmas and New Year the enslaved had about six days without work.

beats.scene: Men pass a bottle among themselves around a holiday table
beats.summary: Most spent the holiday drinking whiskey, which their masters liked best; abstainers were scorned.

beats.scene: Men lie exhausted and ill in the straw after the holidays
beats.summary: Douglass argues that the holidays were a trick to disgust slaves with freedom, and a safety valve.

beats.scene: A well-dressed farmer speaks with a young man at a farm gate
beats.summary: In January 1834 Frederick goes to William Freeland, a fairer man who is no pretender to religion.

beats.scene: Four young men talk quietly behind a barn at dusk
beats.summary: He makes friends among the enslaved men nearby, including Henry and John Harris and Sandy Jenkins.

beats.scene: Young men sit on logs in a woodland clearing with a spelling book
beats.summary: Frederick starts a secret Sunday school to teach his friends to read.

beats.scene: A young teacher points to letters in a book as eager faces lean in
beats.summary: The pupils pay nothing and risk a whipping, yet they come eagerly.

beats.scene: A young man talks warmly with friends under the stars
beats.summary: He loves these friends more than any he has known since; they are brave as well as loving.

beats.scene: A young man looks out over fields at dusk, arms folded
beats.summary: A fairer master only sharpens his wish for freedom.

beats.scene: A young man whispers to a friend beside a haystack at night
beats.summary: He speaks to his pupils about escape, and they agree to try together.

beats.scene: Five young men sit in a dark barn, whispering by a candle
beats.summary: The friends weigh the dangers, even sale to the far South, and agree to risk it.

beats.scene: A large canoe rests on a dark shore under bright stars
beats.summary: The plan: take a canoe at Easter, paddle about seventy miles up the bay, then follow the North Star.

beats.scene: Five men in a canoe look like fishermen on a bright morning
beats.summary: They choose the water route so they may be taken for fishermen, not runaways.

beats.scene: A young man writes slowly at a plain table by candlelight
beats.summary: Frederick writes passes for each man, signed with William Hamilton's name, for the Easter holidays in Baltimore.

beats.scene: Five friends clasp hands in the dark, tense but determined
beats.summary: As the day nears, they promise to stand by one another.

beats.scene: A young man stops, uneasy, in a field at dawn
beats.summary: On the morning, Frederick feels sure that they have been betrayed.

beats.scene: Armed men ride up to a farmhouse as workers stand frozen
beats.summary: William Hamilton arrives with constables and armed men, and they bind the young men.

beats.scene: A young man whispers to his friends as their hands are bound
beats.summary: Frederick whispers to own nothing, and they quietly get rid of the passes.

beats.scene: Angry men question five calm young men outside a grey stone house
beats.summary: Examined at St Michaels, the friends deny everything and there is no proof.

beats.scene: Tied young men march behind a horseman along a dusty road
beats.summary: They are taken to Easton jail, and Frederick, thought the ringleader, expects the worst.

beats.scene: A young man sits alone on a bench in a stone cell
beats.summary: One by one his friends are released, and Frederick is left alone in jail.

beats.scene: A young man walks from a jail beside a stern man in a hat
beats.summary: Thomas Auld does not sell him; he takes Frederick out and sends him to Baltimore.

beats.scene: A young man gazes at a busy harbour from the deck of a sloop
beats.summary: He returns to Hugh and Sophia Auld in Baltimore, determined to try again.

beats.scene: A young man stands at the gate of a busy shipyard as workers hammer
beats.summary: Hugh hires him to Mr Gardner, who is rushing to finish two warships for Mexico.

beats.scene: White carpenters glare at a Black worker across a crowded yard
beats.summary: White carpenters resent Black workers, drive out the free ones and turn on Frederick.

beats.scene: Several young men attack a lone worker with a brick and a heavy tool
beats.summary: Four or five apprentices attack him, and his left eye is badly hurt.

beats.scene: A bandaged young man sits as a woman tends his wounds
beats.summary: Sophia weeps and dresses his wounds, and Hugh is furious.

beats.scene: A magistrate shakes his head at a desk before two visitors
beats.summary: Esquire Watson can do nothing, since no white witness will speak and the law refuses Black testimony.

beats.scene: A shipwright drives caulking iron into a seam of a ship on the dock
beats.summary: Hugh moves him to Walter Price's yard, where he learns caulking quickly.

beats.scene: A young man hands coins to a stern man at a table
beats.summary: He earns six or seven dollars a week, hands it all to Hugh and feels robbed.

beats.scene: A young man asks a stern man for something across a wooden table
beats.summary: In spring 1838 he asks to hire his own time; Thomas refuses, but Hugh agrees for three dollars a week.

beats.scene: A caulker hammers at a ship's hull in falling rain
beats.summary: The bargain is hard, as he pays even when idle or ill, but he prefers it.

beats.scene: Worshippers walk into a camp meeting among tall trees at sunset
beats.summary: In August 1838 he is late with his payment after a camp meeting, and Hugh is angry.

beats.scene: A young man sits silent at work, planning something behind a calm face
beats.summary: Frederick decides it is time to run and tells no one.

beats.scene: A steam train carries a young man north through a green countryside
beats.summary: On 3 September 1838 he escapes, reaching New York without interruption.

beats.scene: A locked door and a sealed letter lie on an empty table
beats.summary: He will not say how he escaped, to protect others and not help slaveholders.

beats.scene: A man stands in a busy New York street with a small bag
beats.summary: In New York he feels like one who has escaped a den of hungry lions.

beats.scene: A lone man sits on a barrel at a dock, wary of strangers
beats.summary: Joy gives way to loneliness and fear of kidnappers; he is a stranger without friends.

beats.scene: A sailor speaks kindly to a young man on a quiet street
beats.summary: A kind sailor asks if he is a fugitive and takes him home.

beats.scene: A man with a kind face welcomes a young traveller into a small office
beats.summary: The sailor brings him to David Ruggles, who helps fugitives.

beats.scene: A young woman steps down from a coach in a busy street
beats.summary: Frederick writes to Anna Murray, a free woman of Baltimore, and she comes to New York.

beats.scene: A minister marries a young couple in a small parlour
beats.summary: They are married by the Reverend James Pennington, and Ruggles gives them a certificate.

beats.scene: A man points at a map of the northern coast beside a lamp
beats.summary: Ruggles thinks New York too dangerous and sends them to New Bedford, Massachusetts.

beats.scene: A stagecoach stops before a neat house in a harbour town
beats.summary: In New Bedford, Nathan Johnson welcomes the couple warmly into his home.

beats.scene: A young man frowns at two name cards on a table
beats.summary: He had dropped Bailey for Johnson, but New Bedford had too many Johnsons.

beats.scene: A man reads a poem aloud as another writes a name
beats.summary: Johnson, reading The Lady of the Lake, suggests Douglass, and he becomes Frederick Douglass.

beats.scene: A thriving harbour with ships, warehouses and people at work
beats.summary: He expected a poor North, but New Bedford was rich and comfortable without slavery.

beats.scene: A man rolls heavy casks along a sunlit dock
beats.summary: He takes any work he can find, and his wages belong to him.

beats.scene: A man reads a printed newspaper by candlelight, his wife beside him
beats.summary: He subscribes to The Liberator, which sets his soul on fire.

beats.scene: A young man stands nervously on a platform before a packed meeting hall
beats.summary: In August 1841 at Nantucket he is urged to speak, and the Society soon hires him.

beats.scene: A man sits at a desk with an open Bible, writing carefully
beats.summary: In an appendix Douglass explains that he is not an enemy of all religion.

beats.scene: Two churches stand side by side, one with chains on its door
beats.summary: He distinguishes the Christianity of Christ, which he loves, from the slaveholding kind, which he hates.

beats.scene: A preacher raises a hand over a congregation seated in neat rows
beats.summary: He accuses slaveholding churches of hypocrisy, and closes with a bitter parody of a hymn.

beats.scene: The author signs the last page of a manuscript in a plain study
beats.summary: He ends hoping the book will throw light on slavery and hasten freedom, signed at Lynn in April 1845.

beats.scene: A bookseller hands a printed book to a customer in a busy shop
beats.summary: The Narrative sells thousands of copies, but it names his owners, and friends fear for his safety.

beats.scene: A man speaks to a large British audience in a grand hall
beats.summary: He spends almost two years in Britain and Ireland, where editions are printed in Dublin.

beats.scene: Friends hand a bag of coins to a man at a desk
beats.summary: British friends pay about 150 pounds to Hugh Auld, and Douglass returns as a free man.

beats.scene: A printing press and a newspaper titled with a star
beats.summary: He starts The North Star in 1847 and speaks for women's rights at Seneca Falls in 1848.

beats.scene: A tall man in a dark coat greets a President in a study
beats.summary: In the Civil War he urges Lincoln to end slavery, helps recruit Black soldiers and meets him.

beats.scene: Young readers share a worn copy of a book in a bright classroom
beats.summary: Douglass dies in 1895; the Narrative is still read as a classic of freedom.

A1A2: William Lloyd Garrison begins the book by remembering a meeting in 1841.
A young man stood up slowly and looked afraid in front of the crowd.
He told the story of his life, and everyone listened without a sound.
Garrison asked the crowd if they had heard a thing or a man.
Soon Douglass was working for a group against slavery and speaking in many towns.
So Douglass wrote his own book, using the real names of people and places.
Garrison says every word is true and nothing in the book is invented.
Wendell Phillips writes a short letter and tells an old story about a lion.
Phillips is glad that slaves can now write their own true history.
Phillips says this book shows what slavery is really like from inside.
Frederick Douglass was born in Maryland, on a small farm near Tuckahoe.
Slaves did not know their birthdays, so they used the seasons instead.
White children knew their ages, and this made young Frederick feel sad.
His father was a white man, but Frederick never knew who he was.
If the mother was a slave, her child was a slave too.
Frederick was taken from his mother before he was one year old.
His mother worked on a farm twelve miles away from his home.
She came at night, lay beside him, and was gone before the morning.
In Tuckahoe, his mother was the only slave who could read.
His mother died when he was about seven, and he was not there.
His grandmother, Betsy Bailey, made fishing nets and grew fine sweet potatoes.
He lived with her in a small cabin until he was about six.
One day she took him on a long walk to a big farm.
At the big farm, he met his brother and sisters, who felt like strangers.
His grandmother left while he played, and Frederick cried bitterly on the ground.
Colonel Lloyd was a rich man with a huge farm beside the Wye.
The farm was like a small village with many kinds of workers.
Each month, a few workers walked to the big house for food.
On the road the men sang loudly, in tones that carried far.
Later he understood that those songs were full of sadness.
Captain Anthony was not thought cruel, but he sometimes beat his slaves.
Captain Anthony ordered his slave Hester to stay away from a young man.
Hester cried out in pain, and Frederick hid in a dark closet.
To Frederick, this was the first gate into the hell of slavery.
Each month, grown slaves got some corn flour and a little pork or fish.
Small children got only two shirts a year and no shoes.
The children had no beds, and Frederick slept inside a corn sack.
The children ate cooked corn from a long wooden trough, like pigs.
Aunt Katy, the cook, sometimes kept hungry children from their food.
Frederick was too young for field work, so he did small jobs.
Colonel Lloyd had a beautiful garden full of apples, pears and peaches.
To stop people taking fruit, the colonel put black tar on the fence.
Any slave with tar on his clothes was whipped, guilty or not.
The colonel's old driver was beaten whatever he did, and could not answer.
One day the colonel met a slave on the road and asked him questions.
Soon after, the honest slave was sold to a trader from Georgia.
After this, slaves learned to say that their masters were kind.
Slaves sometimes fought over whose master was the richest and best.
Mr Severe was a cruel boss, and his name suited him well.
Mr Hopkins was a quieter boss, but he did not stay long.
Mr Gore was proud, clever, and very cruel, and everyone feared him.
Demby, one of the slaves, ran from Mr Gore into a creek.
Gore called three times, then he shot Demby, who fell into the water.
Gore said Demby had to die, or the others would also refuse.
In that county, killing a slave was not treated as a crime.
Miss Lucretia, the master's daughter, kindly gave him bread and butter.
One day he was told he would go to live in Baltimore.
He had to wash in the creek for three whole days.
She promised him a pair of trousers, the first he ever owned.
Frederick sailed to Baltimore on the Sally Lloyd, full of joy.
The boat reached Baltimore, a busy city beside the water.
Sophia Auld met him at the door with a kind smile.
Sophia had never owned a slave, and she worked hard herself.
Sophia kindly taught him the alphabet and some short, easy words.
Hugh Auld found out and told his wife to stop at once.
He said that a slave given an inch would soon take a mile.
Learning would make a slave unhappy and no use to his master.
Frederick finally understood why masters did not want slaves to read.
Then he knew that reading was the road to freedom.
Sophia changed, and she became hard and cold toward him.
In the city, slaves lived better than slaves in the country.
Near the Aulds, a woman was cruel to two slave girls.
Frederick had plenty of bread, and the poor white boys had little.
He took a spelling book on his errands and studied between jobs.
He told the boys they would be free, but he would not.
He lived with the Aulds for about seven years.
At about twelve, Frederick got a book called The Columbian Orator.
In the book, a slave argued with his master and won.
He also read speeches about freedom, by a man named Sheridan.
The more he read, the more he hated the men who owned him.
Learning to read made him sad, for he could see his chains.
He kept hearing a strange word, abolition, and wanted to know what it meant.
He looked in a dictionary, but it did not tell him enough.
A newspaper told him about people who wanted to end slavery.
Two Irish workers told him he should run away to the north.
He listened, but he was afraid they wanted to trick him.
He decided to learn to write, to help him escape one day.
At the shipyard, carpenters marked each timber with a big letter.
He told the boys he could write, and they said he could not.
When the house was empty, he copied words from Tommy's old school books.
Captain Anthony died, and Frederick had to go back to Maryland.
Men, women, and children stood in a line with the farm animals.
He feared being given to Andrew, who was known to be harsh.
He fell to Lucretia and was sent back to Baltimore.
His old grandmother was left alone in a small hut in the woods.
She had cared for the whole family, and now she had nobody.
He asked if God would punish men who did such things.
Lucretia and her brother soon died, and the family broke up.
Thomas Auld had a fight with his brother Hugh and took Frederick away.
In March 1832, Frederick said goodbye to Baltimore and to the Aulds.
Thomas Auld was a mean man, and his slaves were often hungry.
Frederick was so hungry that he sometimes took food in secret.
He believed that taking food from his own master was not stealing.
In August 1832, Thomas Auld went to a religious camp meeting.
Auld prayed three times a day, but he was not kinder.
Auld used the Bible to excuse his cruelty to his slaves.
He found that religious masters were often the worst of all.
He started a Sunday school to teach other slaves to read.
Angry white men came with sticks and broke up the school.
Auld said the city had spoiled Frederick, so he sent him away.
Edward Covey was a poor farmer who broke the spirit of slaves.
On the first day of 1833, Frederick went to live with Covey.
Frederick could not control the wild animals pulling the cart, and Covey whipped him.
Covey made them work from first light until dark, and he whipped Frederick often.
Covey moved quietly through the corn to spy, and the slaves called him the snake.
The hard work and beatings broke his body and his spirit.
On Sundays, he watched the white sails on the great bay.
He spoke to the ships, saying they were free and he was not.
He decided that he would try to run away one day.
Covey prayed loudly each day, yet he was cruel to his workers.
On a very hot August day, Frederick felt ill in the field.
Frederick fell to the ground, and Covey kicked him angrily.
Hurt and bleeding, Frederick walked seven miles through the woods.
Auld said Covey was a good man and sent him back.
He went back, but Covey chased him, so he ran into the woods.
He hid in the woods all day, hungry and afraid.
In the woods, Frederick met Sandy Jenkins, who offered to help him.
Sandy gave him a root and said it would keep him safe.
On Sunday, Covey spoke kindly to him, and Frederick felt confused.
On Monday morning, Covey came to the stable with a rope.
Frederick suddenly decided to fight back, and he grabbed Covey.
Covey was shocked, and he shook as Frederick held him.
Bill Smith refused to help Covey, so the two men fought alone.
They fought for nearly two hours, and then Covey let him go.
Covey never beat Frederick again for the rest of his time there.
That fight was the turning point of his life as a slave.
He told himself he would never again take a beating quietly.
He felt strong again, as if he had come back to life.
He stayed with Covey until Christmas, and nobody beat him.
He did not trust the root, but he trusted his own courage.
At Christmas, slaves were allowed six days without work.
Masters wanted slaves to drink during the holiday, and many did.
The masters hoped the slaves would hate freedom after the holiday.
In 1834, Frederick went to work for a farmer named Freeland.
Frederick worked with other slaves, and he soon made good friends.
Frederick began a secret Sunday school to teach his friends to read.
His pupils wanted to learn so much that they risked a whipping.
Frederick loved his friends more than anyone he had ever known.
Even with a fairer master, Frederick still wanted to be free.
He told his friends about his wish to escape.
They knew the road to freedom was long and very dangerous.
They planned to paddle a big canoe up the bay at night.
On the water, they hoped people would think they were fishermen.
Frederick wrote a note for each man, saying he could travel.
The friends promised to help each other on the dangerous road.
On the morning of the escape, Frederick felt that something was wrong.
Armed men rode up to the farm and seized the young men.
He whispered to his friends to say nothing, and they agreed.
They said they had no plan, and nobody could prove it.
The five young men were taken to the jail in Easton.
His friends went home one by one, but Frederick stayed in jail.
Thomas Auld took Frederick out of jail and did not sell him.
He sailed to Baltimore again and went back to the Aulds.
Hugh Auld sent Frederick to work in a busy shipyard.
Some white workers were angry that Black men worked in the yard.
Four or five white boys attacked him, and his eye was hurt.
Sophia cried when she saw his wounds, and she cared for him.
The law officer said no white man had spoken, so he could do nothing.
Hugh sent him to a new yard to learn a trade.
He earned good money, but he gave all of it to Hugh.
He asked Hugh to let him find his own work.
He paid Hugh three dollars a week and kept the rest.
Frederick went to a camp meeting and was late paying Hugh.
Frederick said nothing to Hugh, but he made his plan.
On the third of September, Frederick left Baltimore, and he was free.
He does not say how he escaped, to protect other slaves.
In New York, he felt joy, like a man who had escaped lions.
But soon he felt alone, and he was afraid to speak.
A kind sailor saw his trouble and took him home.
David Ruggles, who helped runaway slaves, welcomed Frederick into his home.
He wrote to Anna Murray in Baltimore, and she came to him.
Anna and Frederick married in New York a few days later.
Ruggles said New York was unsafe, so they went to New Bedford.
In New Bedford, Nathan Johnson welcomed them into his home.
He had changed his name to Johnson, but New Bedford had too many.
Nathan Johnson was reading a poem, and he suggested the name Douglass.
New Bedford was rich, and it did not use slaves.
He worked hard at many jobs, and his pay was his own.
He read The Liberator every week, and it filled him with hope.
In 1841, at Nantucket, he stood up and spoke to a crowd.
Douglass added an appendix to explain what he said about religion.
He loved true Christianity but hated the religion that defended slavery.
He said that some ministers and church members supported slavery.
He ended the book by hoping it would help end slavery.
The book sold very well and made Douglass famous across the country.
In Britain and Ireland, he gave speeches to large crowds.
British friends paid money so that Douglass could be free.
Douglass started a newspaper called The North Star in 1847.
During the war, he met President Lincoln and spoke with him.
Douglass died in 1895, but people still read his book today.
B1B2: William Lloyd Garrison, the famous editor, wrote the preface to this book and explained why it mattered. He remembered an antislavery meeting on the island of Nantucket in the summer of 1841, where he first heard the author speak.
Douglass had not planned to speak that day, and he came forward slowly. Garrison remembered that he seemed nervous, as any man might who had never stood before so many people.
Frederick spoke about his life as a slave, and the whole room became very quiet. Garrison said that he had never hated slavery so strongly as he did at that moment.
Garrison said that even Patrick Henry never made a more eloquent speech for liberty. Then he asked the crowd whether they had heard a piece of property or a man, and they answered that it was a man.

The Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society asked Douglass to travel and speak for them, and he agreed. Audiences were so impressed by his words that some of them began to doubt that he had ever been a slave.
The title page says that the book was written by himself, and Garrison confirms that this is true. Douglass did not hide behind invented names, because he wanted every fact to be checked.
Garrison says that he is sure the book is true in every statement. Nothing in it is invented or exaggerated, and he believes that it falls short of the full reality of slavery.

After the preface comes a letter from Wendell Phillips, another leading campaigner against slavery. He begins with an old fable: a lion sees a picture of a man beating a lion and says that lions would paint it differently.
Phillips says that he is glad the time has come when the lions write history. Until now, he explains, slavery had mostly been described by the people who had ruled over it.
Phillips says that people in the free states have seen slavery only from the outside. This book, he promises, will take them inside, and Douglass is now ready to begin his story.

Douglass begins his story with a plain fact: he was born in a place called Tuckahoe, in Talbot County, Maryland. It lay near a small town named Hillsborough, on the flat farmland of the Eastern Shore.

Douglass explains that he cannot tell his exact age, and he has never met a slave who could tell his own. They spoke of planting time, harvest time, cherry time, springtime and fall instead of using dates.
The white children around him always knew how old they were, and he envied them. When he asked his master about his own age, the man told him that a slave had no right to ask such a thing.
Douglass tells us that his father was a white man, and people whispered that it was his own master. He never learned whether this was true, because the subject was never spoken about openly.
The law said that a child must follow the condition of its mother. So when a white man had a child with an enslaved woman, the child was born a slave, and the father could own it.
Douglass was separated from his mother when he was still a baby, before he was a year old. This was common, he explains, and it was done so that the love between mother and child would grow weaker.
Harriet Bailey was hired out to work on a farm about twelve miles away. After a long day in the fields, she walked that distance in the dark just to see her son.
She would lie down beside her sleeping son for a few hours and leave before dawn. If she was not in the field at sunrise, she would be whipped.

Harriet Bailey was the only person of her colour in all of Tuckahoe who could read. Douglass wonders where she learned it, and he is proud to think that his own love of learning may have come from her.
Harriet Bailey died when her son was about seven years old. He was not allowed to be with her during her illness, at her death or at her burial.

Frederick's grandmother, Betsy Bailey, was famous in the neighbourhood for making fishing nets and for growing sweet potatoes. Neighbours often asked for her help, because she seemed to succeed where others failed.

On the farms of that district, old women often raised the children while the parents worked elsewhere. Frederick lived in his grandmother's cabin until he was about six, and it was the only home he knew.
One day his grandmother took him on a long journey on foot to Colonel Lloyd's plantation. It was the farm where his master lived, and where Frederick's brother and sisters were already living.

At Colonel Lloyd's, Frederick was told to play with his brother and sisters. They were almost strangers to him, because slave children were kept apart from their families, and they had never lived together.
While Frederick was playing with the other children, his grandmother quietly left. When they told him that she had gone, he threw himself on the ground and cried bitterly.
The plantation belonged to Colonel Edward Lloyd, a very wealthy planter. Its centre, the Great House Farm, stood near the Wye River, and Captain Anthony managed it for him.
The Great House Farm was like a village of its own. It had its own blacksmiths, carpenters, weavers and shoemakers, so the estate hardly needed to buy anything from outside.
Once a month, a few enslaved men were sent from each farm to the Great House Farm to collect the food for the others. To be chosen was a great honour, and the men who went were envied by the rest.
As the chosen men walked towards the Great House Farm, they sang loudly. Their songs were wild and strange, and some of the words made no sense at all.
As a boy, Frederick did not understand that these songs were songs of sorrow. Later, as a free man, he heard in every note a protest against slavery.
Captain Anthony was not known as an especially cruel master. Even so, he sometimes whipped the people he owned in a rage, and he sometimes seemed to take pleasure in it.
Frederick's aunt Hester was a young woman who belonged to Captain Anthony. He had ordered her not to keep company with a young man named Ned Roberts, who lived on Colonel Lloyd's farm.
Early one morning, Captain Anthony tied Hester's hands above her head and whipped her. Her cries were terrible, and Frederick was so frightened that he hid in a closet until it was over.
Douglass calls this scene the blood-stained gate, the entrance to the hell of slavery. He knew that he was about to pass through it, and that this was only the first of many such cruelties.

On Colonel Lloyd's farms, each grown worker received a monthly allowance of about eight pounds of pork or fish and a bushel of cornmeal. For clothing they got, once a year, two coarse shirts, trousers, a jacket, stockings and shoes.
Slave children on the farm were given even less than the adults. They had two coarse shirts a year, and no shoes, stockings, jackets or trousers, so they were often cold.

There were no beds for the slaves, only one coarse blanket for each grown man and woman. The children had nothing, and Frederick sometimes slept in a corn sack, and his feet were cracked by the frost.
The children's food was a cornmeal porridge, which was poured into a large wooden trough on the ground. They ate it with oyster shells, pieces of wood or their hands, and the strongest got the most.
Aunt Katy, the cook in Captain Anthony's kitchen, was a cruel woman. She would sometimes punish a child by taking away his food, and Frederick was often hungry because of her.
Frederick was too young to work in the fields, so he was given small tasks. He drove the cows home in the evening, kept the chickens out of the garden and ran errands for the house.
Colonel Lloyd kept a very large and beautiful garden behind his house. It held fruit of nearly every kind, from the hardy apple of the north to the delicate orange of the south.
To stop people from stealing his fruit, the colonel had the fence around the garden covered with tar. A man who touched it would carry the sticky black mark on his clothes and skin.
Any slave who was found with tar on his body was whipped, whether he had touched the fruit or not. The stain was taken as proof, and few dared to explain.
Colonel Lloyd was proud of his fine horses and carriages. His old coachman, Barney, looked after them well, yet whatever he did, he was blamed and whipped, and he took the blows without a word.
Colonel Lloyd owned so many slaves that he did not know them all by sight. One day he met a man on the road and asked him who his master was and whether he was treated well.
The colonel said nothing, and the man thought no more about it. A short time later he was told that he had been sold to a Georgia trader, for finding fault with his master.
Everyone on the farm learned from this story to be careful with their words. If a stranger asked, a slave would always say that his master was kind and that he had enough to eat.

Douglass saw enslaved men argue, and even fight, over whose master was the richest or the kindest. It was a strange kind of pride, he thought, and it showed how slavery could bend the minds of those it held.
Mr Severe, one of the overseers, was a cruel and hot-tempered man, and his name suited him well. He cursed and swore at the workers, and he whipped them as if he enjoyed it.
After Mr Severe died, his place was taken by Mr Hopkins, a quiet man who seldom spoke and did not whip so often. His time in the post was short, and then Mr Gore took his place.
Mr Gore was proud, ambitious and cruel, and he was exactly the right man for the job. He never allowed a slave to answer back or explain, and he punished the smallest reply.
Demby, an enslaved man, was whipped by Mr Gore for a small fault, and he ran and plunged into a creek. He stood in the water up to his neck and refused to come out.
Mr Gore called to Demby three times, and when he still did not come out, he raised his gun and shot him. Demby fell back into the water, and the other workers watched in horror.

Gore explained that Demby had set a dangerous example, and that if one slave was allowed to refuse, the others would soon follow. Nobody blamed him, and he was never called to answer for what he had done.

Douglass says that the killing of a slave was hardly treated as a crime in that part of Maryland. Other murders of enslaved people had gone unpunished, because the only witnesses were slaves, and their word was not accepted in court.
Lucretia, the daughter of Captain Anthony, was one of the few people who were kind to Frederick. When the cook kept him from his food, she gave him bread and butter.
When Frederick was about eight, Lucretia arranged for him to go to Baltimore. There he would live with Hugh Auld, the brother of her husband, and look after Hugh's little son.
Lucretia told him to wash away the dirt of the farm, or the people in Baltimore would laugh at him. He spent three days scrubbing himself in the creek.
Lucretia promised that if he got himself clean, she would give him a pair of trousers. He had never owned any, because until then he had worn only a long shirt.
At last Frederick sailed away on Colonel Lloyd's sloop, the Sally Lloyd, and he felt nothing but joy. His mother was dead, his grandmother was far away, and nothing on the farm held him there.
The sloop reached Baltimore, and Frederick was taken to the home of Hugh Auld at Fell's Point. It was the first city he had ever seen, and everything in it was new to him.
Sophia Auld, Hugh's wife, welcomed Frederick at the door with a kind smile. He was not used to being met with kindness, and he hardly knew how to answer her.
Sophia Auld had never owned a slave before, and she had once worked for her own living. She was a pious woman with a tender heart, and she treated Frederick like a child, not like property.
Sophia kindly began to teach Frederick the letters of the alphabet. When he knew them, she helped him to spell words of three or four letters.
Hugh Auld soon found out what was happening, and he ordered his wife to stop at once. He told her that it was both unlawful and unsafe to teach a slave to read.
Hugh Auld said that if you give a slave an inch, he will take a mile. A slave, he said, should know nothing except how to obey his master, and learning would only spoil him.
Learning, Hugh Auld said, would make a slave unmanageable and of no value to his master. It would do the slave no good and only make him discontented and unhappy.
These words sank deep into Frederick's heart, and he finally understood something that had always puzzled him. It was how a white man could keep a Black man enslaved.

From that moment, Frederick understood that the road from slavery to freedom went through learning. He called Hugh Auld's speech the first antislavery lecture he had ever heard, and he decided to learn to read at any cost.
Sophia began to follow her husband's rules, and her kind heart slowly changed. If she found Frederick with a newspaper or a book, she would snatch it away from him.
Douglass says that a city slave is almost free compared with a slave on a plantation. He was better fed and clothed, and there was some shame among the masters that checked the worst cruelty.
Near the Aulds lived a woman named Mrs Hamilton, who was very cruel to two enslaved girls, Henrietta and Mary. Her neighbours were so shocked that they reported her to the authorities.
In Baltimore, Frederick had enough to eat, but many of the poor white boys in the street did not. He gave them bread, and in return they gave him lessons in reading.
Frederick carried a small spelling book with him when he was sent on errands. As soon as his work was done, he took it out and studied it, and he often asked the boys for help.
Sometimes Frederick said to the boys that they would be free at twenty-one, while he was a slave for life. He asked them whether he had not as good a right to be free as they did.
Frederick lived in the Aulds' household for about seven years. During that time, he succeeded in learning to read and write, in spite of every rule against it.
When he was about twelve, Frederick got hold of a book called The Columbian Orator. It was a schoolbook of speeches and dialogues, and he read it at every chance he had.
One part of the book was a dialogue between a master and his slave, who had run away three times. The slave answered every argument for slavery so well that his master set him free.
The book also held speeches by Sheridan, who argued for giving Catholics equal rights. Frederick found in them thoughts that he had often had himself but never been able to put into words.
The more Frederick read, the more he hated slavery and the people who kept him in it. His reading had opened his eyes, but it had not shown him a way out.
Frederick felt that learning to read had been a curse as much as a blessing. It had shown him how wretched his situation was, and he sometimes envied the slaves who did not understand it.
Frederick kept hearing the word abolition, but he did not know what it meant. He could tell from the angry voices of the white men who used it that it was important to him.
Frederick looked up the word in a dictionary and found that it meant the act of abolishing. But he still did not know what it was that people wanted to abolish, and he was afraid to ask.
One day a newspaper told him that people in the north were asking Congress to end slavery in the District of Columbia. Now he knew what abolition meant, and he began to see the light.
One day Frederick helped two Irish workmen unload a boat full of stones on the dock. They asked if he was a slave for life, and when he said yes, they told him to run away to the north.
Frederick pretended that he was not interested in what the men had said. He feared that they might be trying to trap him into admitting that he wanted to run, so that they could claim a reward.
From that day, Frederick thought often about escaping to the north. He decided to learn how to write, so that when the time came he could write himself a pass.
Frederick watched the ship carpenters at work in a shipyard near the house. They marked each piece of timber with a letter to show where it belonged on the ship, and he learned the letters.
When he met boys who could write, Frederick said that he could write as well as they could. They doubted it, so he wrote the letters he knew on the fence, and they showed him more.
Tommy Auld had gone to school and left behind copybooks full of neat writing. When Hugh and Sophia were out, Frederick sat at the table and copied every line, again and again.
After several years, Captain Anthony died, leaving a son, Andrew, and a daughter, Lucretia. Frederick was sent for at once, to be valued with the rest of the property.
At the valuation, men and women, old and young, were ranked with horses, sheep and pigs. They were all examined in the same way, as property, and Frederick never forgot it.
Frederick was afraid that he might be given to Andrew Anthony, who was known to be a hard and cruel man. He hoped that he would fall to Lucretia instead, and to his great relief he did.
Lucretia sent Frederick straight back to Baltimore, to Hugh Auld's house. He was glad to return to the city and to the lessons he had left behind.
His grandmother, Betsy Bailey, was now very old, and her strength was almost gone. After a lifetime of service to the family, she was left alone in a small hut in the woods, with a mud chimney.
She had nursed and raised the old master's children and grandchildren. Now, in her old age, she had nobody beside her, because her own family had been scattered.
Douglass asks a stern question: will a righteous God not punish such things? He says that this one case shows what slavery does to people who serve it faithfully.
Not long afterwards, both Lucretia and her brother Andrew died, and their family was broken up. Thomas Auld, Lucretia's husband, soon married again, this time to Rowena Hamilton.
Some time later, Thomas Auld quarrelled with his brother Hugh. In anger, Thomas took Frederick away from Baltimore and sent him to live with him at St Michaels.
In March 1832, Frederick left Baltimore and went to live with Thomas Auld at St Michaels. He was sad to leave the city where he had learned so much, and he did not know what was waiting for him.
At St Michaels, Frederick found that Thomas Auld was a mean master who did not feed his slaves enough. Among slaveholders, Douglass says, meanness of this kind was thought a shameful fault.
Frederick was often hungry at St Michaels, and sometimes he took food in secret from his own master's supplies. He did not feel that he was doing wrong, and he later explained why.
Frederick argued that taking food from his master was not really stealing. Since both he and the food belonged to the same master, he was only moving property from one place to another.

In August 1832, Thomas Auld went to a Methodist camp meeting by the bay, and he came home saying that he had found religion. Frederick hoped that his master might now set his slaves free, or at least be kinder.
Thomas Auld began to pray morning and evening, and he held family prayers in his house. Yet he did not become kinder, and Frederick thought that he had become even more cruel.

Douglass saw his master whip a lame young woman, and then quote a line from the Bible to justify it. The verse said that a servant who knows his master's will and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes.
Douglass came to believe that religious slaveholders were the worst of all. Their religion gave them a cover for their cruelty and made them feel safe in what they did.
At St Michaels, Frederick started a Sunday school, where he taught other enslaved people to read the Bible. Many of them were eager to learn, and for a short time he was happy.
The Sunday school did not last long, because the news soon spread. Some white churchmen came with sticks and stones and drove the students away, saying that slaves should not be taught to read.

Thomas Auld decided that life in the city had spoiled Frederick and made him hard to manage. At the end of the year, he hired him out to Edward Covey, a farmer known for breaking the spirit of young slaves.
Edward Covey was a poor farmer who rented his land, and he had a name for breaking young slaves. He was also a church member, a class leader who made a show of being very religious.
On the first day of January 1833, Frederick left St Michaels and went to live on Covey's farm. It was about seven miles away, and he went there with a heavy heart.
In his first week, Covey sent Frederick to the woods with a pair of wild oxen, though he had never driven oxen before. They ran away and smashed the cart, and Covey whipped him for it.
Covey worked his people from the first light of day until the last ray had gone, in all kinds of weather. They were given enough food, but hardly any time to eat it.
Covey had a habit of creeping through the fields on his hands and knees to spy on his workers. They called him the snake, and he would suddenly rise up and shout to make them work harder.
After months of hard work and beatings, Frederick felt broken in body, soul and spirit. He no longer wanted to read, and the cheerful spark in his eyes had died.
On Sundays, when he could rest, Frederick stood on the high bank of Chesapeake Bay and watched the white sails of the ships go by. To him they seemed like ghosts that reminded him of his chains.
Frederick spoke to the ships as if they could hear him. He told them that they were free and he was a slave, and that he wished that he could go with them.
Frederick told himself that he would run away one day. He said that he had only one life to lose, and that he would rather be killed running than die standing still.
Covey was a church leader, and he led his family in loud prayers every morning and evening. Douglass saw no sign that his religion had made him kinder to the people who worked for him.
On one of the hottest days of August 1833, Frederick was working with other men, fanning wheat. He began to feel dizzy and sick, and his strength suddenly left him.
Frederick felt his strength go, and he collapsed and fell to the ground. Covey came over, kicked him in the side, and ordered him to get up, but he was too weak to stand.
Frederick decided to go to his master, Thomas Auld, to ask for protection. He walked about seven miles through the woods, bleeding and weak, and he was afraid that he might fall.
Thomas Auld listened a little, then said that Covey was a good man and that Frederick must return to him. If he stayed away, Auld said, he would lose the whole year's wages.
Frederick went back to Covey's farm the next morning, as he had been told. Covey came out after him with a cowskin whip, so Frederick ran for the woods and hid.
Frederick spent the rest of the day in the woods, hungry, hurt and unsure what to do. If he went back, he would be beaten, and if he stayed away, he would be hunted.
While hiding, Frederick met Sandy Jenkins, an enslaved man whose wife was free. Sandy took him to his home, gave him something to eat, and listened to his story.
Sandy told Frederick to carry a certain root in his right pocket. He said that as long as Frederick had it with him, no white man would be able to whip him.
On Sunday morning, Frederick walked back to the farm. On the way he met Covey, who was dressed for church, and the farmer greeted him kindly and sent him to his work.
On Monday morning, Frederick was working in the stable, feeding the horses. Covey crept in quietly behind him with a rope, and suddenly seized his legs, meaning to tie him.
At that moment, Frederick decided to fight back, though he did not know where the courage came from. He seized Covey hard by the throat, and the two men held on to each other.
Covey was so surprised by this resistance that he trembled all over. He asked Frederick whether he meant to go on resisting, and Frederick answered that he did, whatever might happen.

Covey called for help, and a worker named Hughes tried to tie Frederick, but Frederick kicked him away. Then Covey called on Bill Smith, a hired worker, who refused, saying he was hired to work and not to whip.
The two men struggled on the stable floor for nearly two hours. At last Covey let him go, out of breath, and said he would not have whipped Frederick half so much had he not resisted.
For the six months that Frederick stayed with Covey, the farmer never again laid a hand on him in anger. Douglass thought that Covey was afraid of losing his reputation as a breaker of slaves.
Douglass calls the fight with Covey the turning point of his life as a slave. It brought back his self-confidence and his pride, and it made him feel like a man again.
Frederick resolved that, although he might remain a slave in name, he would never again be one in fact. He let it be known that any white man who tried to whip him would have to fight to the end.
Douglass describes the feeling as a resurrection from the tomb of slavery. His crushed spirit rose again, his fear left him, and bold defiance took its place.
Frederick stayed on Covey's farm until Christmas, when his year was over. The work was still hard, but nobody beat him again, and he was glad when the year ended.
Frederick never believed that Sandy's root had any power. What had changed his life, he knew, was his own decision to stand up and fight.
Between Christmas and New Year, the slaves were given about six days without work. They could play games, visit their families or rest, and these days felt like their own.
Many slaves spent the holiday drinking whiskey, and their masters were happy to see it. A slave who worked through the holiday, or who refused to drink, was looked down on.
Douglass believed that the masters planned this on purpose. They wanted the slaves to become sick of drink, and of what they thought freedom was, and glad to return to work.
On the first of January 1834, Frederick went to work for William Freeland. Freeland was a fairer man than Covey, and he gave his workers enough food and enough time to eat it.
Frederick made friends among the enslaved men of the neighbourhood, including Henry Harris, John Harris and Sandy Jenkins. They worked together, trusted one another, and shared whatever they had.
Frederick began a Sunday school again, teaching his friends from the neighbouring farms to read. It had to be done in secret, because many white people would have stopped it at once.
Frederick's pupils were poor and tired, and they could pay him nothing. They came out of love of learning, and he was glad to teach them.
Frederick felt a love for these friends that was stronger than any he had known since. They were not only loving, he says, but brave.
Freeland was a better master than the others, but Frederick was still a slave. A kind master could not satisfy his wish for freedom, and it grew stronger every day.
Frederick spoke to his friends about freedom, and he found that they felt as he did. They all agreed that they would try to escape together.
Frederick and his friends talked for weeks about the dangers of escape. They might be caught, beaten and sold far away, but they agreed that they would rather risk everything than remain slaves.
Their plan was to take a large canoe on the Saturday night before Easter. They would paddle about seventy miles to the head of Chesapeake Bay, set the canoe adrift, and walk north by the North Star.
They chose the water route because they were less likely to be stopped as runaways. They hoped that anyone who saw them would take them for fishermen going about their work.
Frederick wrote a pass for each man, saying that his master had given him leave to spend the Easter holidays in Baltimore. He signed it with the name of William Hamilton, who lived near St Michaels.
As the day drew near, the friends grew nervous but determined. They promised to stand by one another, whatever happened.
On the morning they were to leave, Frederick was working in the field when he felt sure that something was wrong. He told his friends that he believed they had been betrayed.
Soon afterwards, William Hamilton rode up to the farm with two constables and some other men. They seized Frederick and his friends and tied their hands with rope.
As they were being tied, Frederick whispered to his friends to own nothing and deny everything. In the confusion, they quietly got rid of the passes, so that no proof would be found.
The young men were questioned at St Michaels before a group of angry white men. Each of them denied that there had ever been a plan, and nobody could produce any proof.
The young men were taken, tied together, to the county jail in Easton. Frederick feared that he would be sold far away, and that he might never see his friends again.
One by one, the other young men were taken out of jail by their masters. Frederick was left behind, alone in his cell, and he thought that he might be sold.
To his surprise, Thomas Auld came to the jail and took Frederick out. He had not sold him, and he decided instead to send him back to Baltimore, to live again with Hugh Auld.
Frederick returned to Baltimore, to Hugh Auld's house at Fell's Point. He was glad to be back in the city, though he missed the friends he had left in Talbot County.
Hugh Auld sent Frederick to work in a shipyard owned by Mr Gardner, who was building two large warships for the Mexican government. Frederick was supposed to help the carpenters and learn the work.

The white carpenters were angry that free Black men worked in the yard, and said that they were taking the bread from their mouths. They drove away the free Black carpenters, and then they turned on Frederick.
