One day four or five of the white apprentices attacked Frederick together. They hit him with bricks and a heavy tool, and his left eye was badly hurt.
Frederick went home to the Aulds, covered with blood. Sophia, who had grown cold towards him, wept when she saw his wounds, and she dressed them with great tenderness.

Hugh Auld took Frederick to Esquire Watson, a magistrate, to ask for a warrant against the attackers. Watson said that he could do nothing unless a white person would swear to what had happened, and no white person would.
Hugh Auld moved Frederick to another shipyard, owned by Walter Price. There he learned to caulk, which means to seal the seams of a ship with tarred fibre so that no water can come in.
Frederick earned six or seven dollars a week, and every Saturday he gave all of it to Hugh Auld. Hugh sometimes gave him a few cents back, saying that this would encourage him.
In the spring of 1838, Frederick asked for the right to hire his own time. Thomas Auld refused, but Hugh Auld agreed, so long as Frederick paid him three dollars every week.
Frederick worked hard to find jobs and to pay his three dollars every week. It was a hard bargain, since he paid even when ill or without work, but he liked being his own master.
In August 1838, Frederick went to a religious camp meeting outside Baltimore. He came back a little late with his weekly payment, and Hugh Auld was very angry.
Frederick decided that the time had come to run. He worked as usual and gave no sign of what he meant to do, and he told nobody about his plan.
On 3 September 1838, Frederick left Baltimore and reached New York without any trouble. He later wrote that he had left his chains behind him.
Douglass does not say how he escaped from Baltimore. He explains that telling the story would help slaveholders to stop others and would put his helpers in danger.
When Frederick reached New York, he felt like a man who had escaped from a den of hungry lions. He was free, and no one could take his wages from him.
Soon the joy gave way to loneliness and fear. Frederick was free, but he was a stranger without friends or money, and he dared not speak to anyone in case they were kidnappers.
Frederick stayed in this unhappy state for some time, afraid and alone. Then a kind sailor saw that he was in trouble, asked him whether he was a runaway, and took him to a place of safety.
The sailor brought Frederick to David Ruggles, a Black abolitionist who helped fugitives in New York. Ruggles welcomed him warmly and gave him food, shelter and good advice.
Frederick wrote to Anna Murray, a free woman of Baltimore whom he hoped to marry, and asked her to join him. She travelled to New York at once, and they were reunited.
A few days after Anna arrived, they were married by the Reverend James Pennington, a Black minister. Ruggles gave them a certificate, so that the marriage would be on record.
Ruggles thought that New York was too dangerous for a fugitive, so he advised the couple to go to New Bedford, in Massachusetts. They left almost at once, with very little money.
In New Bedford, the couple were taken to the house of Nathan Johnson, a Black abolitionist. He and his wife welcomed them warmly and took a deep interest in their welfare.

To avoid being traced, Frederick had already dropped the name Bailey and called himself Frederick Johnson. But there were so many Johnsons in New Bedford that it was hard to tell them apart, so he needed a new name again.

Nathan Johnson had just been reading The Lady of the Lake, a poem by Sir Walter Scott. He suggested the name Douglass, after a hero in the poem, and from then on the fugitive was known as Frederick Douglass.
Frederick had expected the free North to be poor, but New Bedford was full of ships, warehouses and fine houses. The people there lived more comfortably than most of the slaveholders he had known.
Frederick took whatever work he could find in New Bedford. He sawed wood, shovelled coal, dug cellars and rolled heavy barrels, and he was proud that his wages belonged to him.
Frederick subscribed to The Liberator, the antislavery newspaper edited by William Lloyd Garrison. He read it with great joy, and he said that the paper became his meat and drink.

In August 1841, Frederick attended an antislavery meeting on Nantucket, where he was urged to speak. He felt very nervous, but his first speech made such an impression that he was soon hired as a speaker.
After finishing his story, Douglass decided to add a short appendix. He had written harshly about religion, and he feared that readers might think he was an enemy of all faith.

Douglass says that he sees the widest possible difference between the Christianity of this land and the Christianity of Christ. He loves the pure and peaceful kind, and so he hates the corrupt, slaveholding religion that he calls a fraud.

Douglass says that many preachers in the slave states bought, sold and whipped human beings while claiming to follow Christ. He ends the appendix with a bitter parody of a hymn that mocks such pious hypocrites.
Douglass ends the book by hoping that it will shed light on slavery and hasten the day of freedom for millions. He signs it with his name, from Lynn, Massachusetts, in April 1845.
The Narrative sold very well, and thousands of copies were bought within months. But it also named his former owners, so his friends feared that he might be seized and sent back to slavery.

Douglass spent almost two years in Britain and Ireland, speaking to large audiences about the horrors of slavery. In Ireland, a new edition of his Narrative was printed in Dublin, and it was widely read.
Friends in Britain, among them Ellen Richardson, raised about 150 pounds and paid it to Hugh Auld for Douglass's freedom. In 1847 he returned to America, free from the danger of being seized.
In 1847, Douglass began his own newspaper, The North Star, in Rochester, New York. A year later he spoke for women's right to vote at the Seneca Falls convention.
During the Civil War, Douglass urged President Abraham Lincoln to end slavery and to let Black men fight as soldiers. He helped to recruit them, and he met Lincoln at the White House more than once.
Douglass died in Washington on 20 February 1895, after a long career as a speaker, writer and public servant. His Narrative is still read today, in schools and homes around the world.
C1C2: The book opens not with its author but with a friend, William Lloyd Garrison, the editor of The Liberator and one of the boldest enemies of slavery in America. In his preface he goes back to the summer of 1841, to an antislavery meeting on the island of Nantucket. It was there, he says, that he first heard the voice of Frederick Douglass, and the memory had not faded in four years.

Douglass was a stranger to most of the audience, and he had not expected to speak at all. Garrison recalls that he rose with hesitation and embarrassment, as a sensitive man naturally would in so new and so strange a position. Nobody in the hall could have guessed that this nervous young fugitive was about to move every person who heard him.

As Douglass described what he had lived through, the crowd listened in a silence that Garrison would never forget. He wrote that the speech stirred him more deeply than almost anything he had heard, and that his hatred of slavery had never burned so fiercely. The wrong done to its victims, he realised, was an offence against everything that makes a human being human.

Garrison rose and said that Patrick Henry, the famous voice of the American Revolution, had never made a speech more eloquent in the cause of liberty than the one they had just heard. He then asked the audience whether they had been listening to a thing, to a piece of property, or to a man. The whole hall answered, as with one voice, that they had been listening to a man, and not to a thing.

The Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society soon hired Douglass as a lecturer, and he travelled through the northern states telling his story to crowds who had never heard such a voice. His eloquence, however, bred a strange suspicion, for many listeners found it hard to believe that a man who spoke so well had ever been held in bondage. Garrison saw that only the plain facts, set down in writing and open to every challenge, could silence such doubts.

Garrison assures readers that the work is entirely Douglass's own, which is why the title page proudly declares that it was written by himself. Unlike many earlier stories of escape, it gives the real names of masters, the real places and the real dates. That openness was a dangerous gamble for a man who was still, in the eyes of the law, another person's property.

Garrison declares himself confident that the narrative is essentially true in all its statements, and that nothing has been set down in malice or drawn from the imagination. If it errs at all, he says, it errs by falling short of the reality rather than by overstating a single fact about slavery. Having dated his preface in May 1845, he steps aside and leaves the stage to the author.

Next comes a letter from Wendell Phillips, a gifted speaker and another leader of the antislavery movement, who reminds Douglass of the old fable of the man and the lion. In the story, a lion is shown a picture of a man defeating a lion, and he remarks that the scene would look very different if lions could paint. Phillips uses the tale to make a point about who has always been allowed to tell the story of slavery.

Phillips tells Douglass that he is glad the time has come when the lions write history. For too long, he suggests, the story of slavery had been told by owners, travellers and politicians, while those who suffered it had no means of being heard. Douglass, he adds, had now taken the pen into his own hand, and could tell the truth as only a witness can.

Phillips closes his letter with praise for a man who, by writing this book, has risked his safety to reach the conscience of the nation. Most readers in the free states, he says, have only glimpsed slavery from the outside, and this account will lead them through the door. With that, the introductions end, and Douglass himself steps forward to tell where and how his life began.

Douglass begins, as many life stories do, with the place of his birth, a district called Tuckahoe in Talbot County, Maryland, not far from the little town of Hillsborough. It was a flat and sandy corner of the Eastern Shore, far from the cities of the north and from any road to freedom. He gives these facts plainly, as a witness giving evidence, because he wants every reader to know exactly where to look.

Of his own age he can say very little, for the slaves he grew up among kept time by the work of the farm rather than by the calendar. A man might say that something happened in planting time, in harvest time, in cherry time, in springtime or in the fall, but never on a certain date. Douglass says that he never met a single slave who could tell the day on which he was born.

Even as a small boy he noticed that white children could tell their ages, and he felt the lack of that simple knowledge as a quiet grief. When he dared to ask his master, he was told that such questions were improper and impertinent, the sign of a restless spirit. The refusal was no accident, for the system worked best when the enslaved knew as little about themselves as possible.

His father, Douglass says, was a white man, and it was whispered among the slaves that his own master was the man. He could never confirm the rumour, and the question was one that nobody dared to discuss openly. All he knew for certain was that the world had given him a father it would not name, and a mother who could not stay.

Under the law of Maryland, as in the other slave states, a child took the condition of its mother, so the child of an enslaved woman was born enslaved whoever the father might be. This cruel rule meant that a slaveholder could become the owner of his own children and profit from them. Douglass points out that it gave slaveholders a profit in a wrong that they claimed to condemn.

Before Frederick was a year old, he was taken from his mother and given to the care of his grandmother, as was the usual custom on the farms of that district. Douglass understood the purpose of the custom only later, which was to blunt the natural affection between mother and child. It is a cruelty, he writes, that his mother had no power to refuse.

His mother, Harriet Bailey, had been hired out to a farmer twelve miles away, and she saw her son only by making a journey that would have broken most people. After the work of the day was done, she walked that whole distance in the dark, along lonely roads, simply to look at him. She did it knowing that she must be back at her post by sunrise.

Douglass says that he saw his mother no more than four or five times in his whole life, and always at night. She would lie down beside him, soothe him to sleep, and be gone again before the light came, for a field worker who was not at her place at sunrise could expect the whip. He never saw her face by daylight, and he knew her only as a presence in the dark.

His mother, he discovered long afterwards, was the only person of colour in the whole district of Tuckahoe who could read. How she had learned, in a place where such learning was forbidden, he never knew, and the mystery made him wonder at her all the more. Douglass is proud to think that his own love of letters may have come from her, though she never lived to teach it.

Harriet Bailey died when her son was about seven years old, and he was not permitted to be present during her illness, at her death or at her burial. Douglass admits that when the news reached him, he felt much as he might have felt at the death of a stranger, for the long separation had left them hardly acquainted. It is one of the quietest and saddest admissions in the whole book, and he makes it without any complaint.

Frederick's grandmother, Betsy Bailey, was a woman of real standing in the neighbourhood, for she made the best fishing nets in the district and had a rare talent for growing sweet potatoes. Neighbours sought her out at planting time, convinced that her hands brought a luck that nobody else could match. Douglass remembers her with a pride that the passing years never dimmed, even after all that slavery did to her.

It was the custom on those farms for old women, who were past hard labour, to raise the children whose mothers had been hired away or sent to distant fields. Frederick therefore grew up in his grandmother's small cabin, and for about six years it was the only home he had ever known. He did not yet grasp what it meant to belong to a master, and the shadow of slavery had barely touched that little room.

When Frederick was about six, his grandmother took him by the hand and set out on foot for Colonel Lloyd's plantation, a journey of many weary miles. It was the home of his master, Captain Anthony, and the place where his brother and sisters were already living. Neither the old woman nor the boy could have known how much that long road would change his life.

At the great plantation Frederick was introduced to his brother and sisters, and he was told to play with them. They were hardly more than strangers to him, for the same custom that had parted him from his mother had scattered the children of the family across different farms. Douglass observes that the bond between brothers and sisters had been weakened before it had a chance to grow.

While Frederick was busy playing, his grandmother slipped away without a word, and it was his brother and sisters who told him that she had gone. He remembers throwing himself on the ground and weeping bitterly, a child who had lost the only home he knew. It was, he suggests, his first lesson in the grief that slavery could bring.

The estate belonged to Colonel Edward Lloyd, a wealthy planter whose lands lay along the Wye River, and its heart was the Great House Farm where he lived. Captain Anthony, Frederick's master, did not own the land but managed it, acting as Lloyd's chief agent over a great many enslaved workers. To a small boy, the whole place seemed less like a farm than like a country with its own rulers.

The home plantation was almost a little town, with workshops for every trade the estate required, and craftsmen to fill them. There were blacksmiths and carpenters, weavers and shoemakers, so that the colonel's wealth depended very little on anything outside his own boundaries. Everything that kept the place alive, however, depended on the labour of people who were never paid for it.

Once a month, men were chosen from every outlying farm to walk to the Great House Farm and carry back the allowance of food for their fellow workers. To be sent on that errand was thought a high honour, and the men who earned it were envied and admired by the rest. They felt, Douglass says, rather as officials might feel on a journey to the capital of a country.

As the chosen men set out along the road, they sang, and their voices rose so loud and wild that the woods for miles around rang with them. The songs seemed to Frederick a mixture of the highest joy and the deepest sadness, and many of their words appeared to mean nothing at all. Some of the singers made up their lines as they walked, pouring into them whatever they felt at that moment.

It was only later, when he looked back as a free man, that Douglass understood the true meaning of those songs. Every tone, he says, was a testimony against slavery and a prayer to God for deliverance from chains, and even years afterwards the memory could bring tears to his cheeks as he wrote. Anyone who believes that a singing slave must be a contented slave, he adds, has misunderstood the song, for the slaves sang most when they were most unhappy.

Captain Anthony was not considered an especially cruel master by the standards of that country. Yet Douglass remembers that he could whip an enslaved person in a fit of passion, and that he sometimes seemed to take a kind of pleasure in the act. It was the first lesson the small boy learned about a power that nobody ever checked.

Hester, an aunt of Frederick's, was a young woman who belonged to Captain Anthony, and she had angered him by keeping company with Ned Roberts, a young man from Colonel Lloyd's farm. The captain had forbidden it in plain words, and when she disobeyed him, he flew into a rage. No law, and no neighbour, stood between the young woman and the anger of the man who owned her.

Early one morning Captain Anthony tied Hester's hands above her head and whipped her, and her cries rang through the house. Frederick, who was only a child, was so terrified that he hid in a closet and did not dare to come out until the punishment was over. He writes that he wishes he could set down on paper what he felt, but that the words will not come.

He calls the moment the blood-stained gate, the entrance to the hell of slavery, through which he was about to pass. It was, he says, the first of a long series of such outrages that he would witness, and it taught him that the body of an enslaved person was not his or her own. He tells the story early in the book because he wants readers to feel, as he did, what the gate looks like from the inside.

The monthly allowance for each grown worker on the estate was about eight pounds of pork, or its equivalent in fish, and a bushel of cornmeal, which was meant to last the whole month. Once a year each was also given a few coarse garments, two linen shirts, trousers, a jacket, stockings and a pair of shoes. If any of it failed before the next allowance, the worker simply went without.

The children, boys and girls alike, received only two coarse linen shirts a year, and when these were worn out they went without until the next allowance. They had no shoes, no stockings, no jackets and no trousers, and they were often seen almost naked even in the coldest weather. Douglass states these facts without anger, because, he suggests, the facts speak for themselves.

Nobody on the estate was given a bed of any kind, not even a mattress of straw. The men and women had a single coarse blanket each, but the children had none, and Frederick took to creeping into a corn sack, with his head inside it and his feet out in the cold. His feet, he says, were so cracked by the frost that a pen could have been laid in the cracks.

The children were fed on a coarse porridge of boiled cornmeal, which was poured into a long wooden trough and set on the ground like feed for pigs. They were called to it and ate with oyster shells, with pieces of shingle or simply with their hands, and the strongest and swiftest took the most. Few of them left the trough satisfied, and most were hungry again before the next meal.

Aunt Katy, the cook in Captain Anthony's kitchen, was a woman of violent temper who ruled over the supply of food as if it were her own kingdom. When she was displeased with Frederick, she kept him from his share for the whole day, so that he went hungry until night. A small boy with no one to appeal to could do nothing but wait for her anger to pass.

Being too young for the fields, Frederick was kept busy with the small tasks of a household that never stopped asking for something. He drove the cows home at the end of the day, kept the fowls out of the garden and ran errands to the Great House. His life was easier than the field hands', but he was still a child whose time, like everything else, belonged to someone else.

Colonel Lloyd's garden was one of the wonders of the district, and it held fruit of nearly every kind, from the hardy apple of the north to the delicate orange of the south. For the hungry people who worked beside it every day, it was a temptation that was almost impossible to resist. The colonel, who knew this very well, resolved to guard it with a trick.

Colonel Lloyd's answer to the problem was to have the whole fence tarred from top to bottom, so that anyone who climbed or leaned against it would carry the black stain away with him. The tar was a silent witness that could not be argued with, and a worker who touched it by accident was as exposed as one who had climbed it. Everyone on the estate understood at once what the tar meant, and nobody dared to test it.

Any slave found with tar upon his person was sure to be whipped, since the colonel took the stain as proof that he had been in the garden. Whether the man had really touched the fruit, or had merely brushed against the fence, was a question that nobody asked. The result was that the garden was guarded as much by fear as by the fence itself.

Colonel Lloyd was as proud of his horses and carriages as of anything he owned, and he put them in the care of an old coachman called Barney. Whatever Barney did was wrong, for the colonel could always find some fault in the way a horse was fed or driven, and the punishment for it was a whipping. The old man received the blows in silence, since a slave who tried to explain was accused of insolence, and the penalty for that was worse.

So many people worked for Colonel Lloyd that he could not recognise them all by sight, and one day he met a man on the road whom he did not know. Riding beside him, the colonel asked him who his master was, whether he was well treated, and whether he was given enough to eat. The man, who did not know that he was speaking to his own owner, answered each question truthfully.

Colonel Lloyd said nothing at all, and the man went on his way, thinking no more about it. Within a month or two, however, he was told that he had been sold to a Georgia trader, and the reason given was that he had had the impudence to find fault with his master. To be sold south, away from family and friends, was among the most feared punishments that a slave in Maryland could face.

The story spread quickly across the whole estate and taught its lesson well to everyone who heard it. It is partly for this reason, Douglass explains, that slaves, when questioned about their conditions and their masters, almost always say that they are contented and that their masters are kind. A man who tells a stranger the truth may be the one who is made to pay for it.

He noticed a curious habit among the enslaved on neighbouring estates, who would quarrel, and even come to blows, over which of their masters was the wealthiest, the wisest or the most generous. Douglass saw in this a bitter sign of how slavery could twist the minds of those it held, teaching them to take pride in the very people who held them in chains. Such loyalty, he suggests, was partly fear, and partly a hunger for something to be proud of.

Mr Severe, the overseer, was a man whose name described him exactly, a hard and violent character who was always cursing, swearing and flying into passions. He seemed to take pleasure in punishing, and the workers dreaded the sight of him coming across a field. When he died, Douglass tells us, the enslaved people saw it as a merciful act of Providence.

After Mr Severe came Mr Hopkins, a very different man, who spoke little, whipped rarely and had none of his predecessor's love of cruelty. Even so, he was an overseer, and nobody on the estate was ever allowed to forget it. He did not stay long in the post, and the man who succeeded him was one whom the workers came to fear far more than either.

Mr Gore was proud, ambitious and cruel, and Douglass says that he was exactly the man for such a post, as the post was exactly the place for such a man. He demanded complete submission, and no slave was allowed to answer back, to explain or to defend himself against an accusation. To reply at all, in his eyes, was a crime worse than any fault in the work.

One day Mr Gore began to whip a slave named Demby, and Demby, who could bear no more, broke away and ran into a nearby creek. He stood in the water up to his neck, and he would not come out, though Gore, standing on the bank, ordered him to. No one on the bank had any doubt about what this was: a man refusing, for once, to obey.

Mr Gore called to Demby once, then a second time and then a third, and when the man still stayed where he was, the overseer raised his gun and fired. Within a moment Demby was dead, and the other slaves stood watching in helpless horror. Douglass, then a boy on the estate, learned of it from those who had watched, and he sets it down in the plainest words he can find.

Gore's defence was that Demby had become unmanageable and had set a dangerous example, for if one slave were allowed to defy an overseer without being punished, the rest would soon follow his lead. That argument, absurd as it sounds to us now, satisfied almost everyone among the white people who heard it. Mr Gore was never called to answer for the killing, and he was not even dismissed from his post.

Douglass states that in Talbot County the killing of a slave was not treated as a crime, either by the courts or by the community. Other murders had gone unpunished before Demby's, and the reason was simple: the only people who saw them were often slaves, and the law refused to accept the testimony of a Black person against a white one. In such a system, he implies, justice for the enslaved was not merely slow but altogether impossible.

Among the few kind people Frederick met on the estate was Lucretia, Captain Anthony's daughter, who had married Thomas Auld. When the cook kept him hungry, she would give him a slice of bread and butter, and she showed him a tenderness that was rare in that house. He never forgot her gentleness, and in his book he writes of her with real warmth and gratitude.

When Frederick was about eight years old, Lucretia arranged for him to be sent to Baltimore, to live with Hugh Auld, the brother of her husband Thomas. He was to look after Hugh's small son and run errands about the house, tasks that a boy of his age could manage well enough. For Frederick, the news was a change from a hard place to an unknown one, and he welcomed it.

Before he could leave, Lucretia told him that he must wash himself thoroughly, because the people of Baltimore would laugh at a boy who arrived with the dirt of the plantation on him. For three days Frederick scrubbed himself in the creek until the grime and the dead skin were gone from his feet and knees. It was a small task, but it felt like the first step of a new life.

As a reward for his labour, Lucretia promised Frederick a pair of trousers, a garment he had never worn, for until then he had known only a rough linen shirt that reached to his knees. The promise delighted him more than the journey itself, and he scrubbed all the harder to earn them. It is a small detail, but it shows how little it took to make a child on that estate happy.

On the appointed day Frederick went aboard Colonel Lloyd's sloop, the Sally Lloyd, and sailed away from the plantation without a single regret. His mother was dead, his grandmother lived far away, and his brother and sisters were almost strangers, so nothing held him to the place. Standing at the bow as the shore slid by, he looked towards the unknown city of Baltimore, and he later wrote that this moment was the first plain sign of the kind providence that guided his life.

The sloop carried Frederick up the Chesapeake to Baltimore, and he was taken to the home of Hugh Auld in Fell's Point, the busy shipbuilding district beside the harbour. After the quiet fields of the Eastern Shore, the noise of the wharves and the rows of brick houses were a world that he had never imagined. He was about to begin a new part of his life, and he did not yet know how much it would teach him.

Sophia Auld, Hugh's wife, met the little boy at the door with a face full of kindness, and Frederick, who was used to harsh looks, hardly knew how to answer it. She showed him where he was to live, and she introduced him to her small son Thomas, whom he was to care for. It was a welcome that he remembered with gratitude, even after what came later.

Sophia Auld had never before owned a slave, and before her marriage she had earned her own bread by her own labour, so she knew nothing of the habits of command. She was a pious woman with a tender heart, and she treated the new boy with a gentleness that surprised him. Douglass says that she did not yet understand what slavery would one day do to her.

Without a thought that she was doing anything wrong, Sophia kindly began to teach Frederick the letters of the alphabet. When he had mastered them, she helped him to spell words of three or four letters, and he progressed steadily. For the first time in his life, he held the key to the written word in his own hands.

The lessons did not last long, for Hugh Auld soon discovered what was going on and at once forbade his wife to continue. He told her, among other things, that it was unlawful as well as unsafe to teach a slave to read. Sophia, who had meant nothing but good, was troubled by his anger but did as she was told.

If you give a slave an inch, Hugh Auld told his wife, he will take an ell. A slave, he insisted, ought to know nothing except how to obey his master and do as he was told, and learning would spoil even the best of them. Frederick, who was close enough to hear, overheard every word of it and never forgot any of them.

If the boy learned to read, Hugh Auld declared, there would be no keeping him, for it would forever unfit him to be a slave. He would become unmanageable and worthless to his master, and for himself it could do no good and a great deal of harm, since it would make him discontented and unhappy. Every word of the speech, though meant to defend slavery, was an unintended compliment to the power of knowledge.

Hugh Auld's words sank deep into Frederick's heart and stirred up thoughts that he had never had before. He suddenly understood what had been to him a most perplexing difficulty, namely, the power of the white man to enslave the Black man. Slavery, he saw, did not rest only on whips and chains, but on keeping its victims ignorant.

From that moment, Frederick says, he understood the pathway from slavery to freedom, and he called Hugh Auld's angry speech the first antislavery lecture he had ever heard. What his master most feared, he reasoned, was exactly what he himself most needed, and so he made up his mind to learn to read at any cost. It was a decision made quietly, by a young boy, and it would shape everything that followed.

Sophia, who had been so gentle, soon came to believe her husband's rule as firmly as he did, and she grew watchful and stern. If she found Frederick with a book or a newspaper in his hand, she would rush at him and snatch it away, suspicious of every sheet of paper. Douglass saw in this change a lesson about slavery itself, which could turn a tender heart to stone in the one who held power.

A city slave, Douglass explains, is almost a free man when compared with a slave on a plantation, for he is better fed and clothed and enjoys privileges that are unknown in the country. There is a vestige of decency in the city, a sense of shame before one's neighbours, that checks the worst outbreaks of cruelty. Slaveholders there did not like their neighbours to think that they starved or beat the people they owned.

In a house near the Aulds lived Mrs Hamilton, who treated two enslaved girls, Henrietta and Mary, with a cruelty that shocked the whole street. Her neighbours were so disturbed by what they saw and heard that they complained to the authorities. Douglass tells the story as an example of how, in a city, public opinion could sometimes act as a small check on the worst abuse.

In the Aulds' house Frederick was never short of bread, while many of the poor white boys he met in the streets were often hungry. So he made a bargain with them, and when he was sent on an errand he would carry bread in his pocket and give it to them. In return, they paid him with what Douglass calls the more valuable bread of knowledge, a few letters and words at a time.

Whenever he was sent on an errand, Frederick carried a small spelling book in his pocket, and as soon as the task was done he would sit down and study it. His teachers were the poor white boys in the street, and their lessons were given in doorways and on wharves rather than in any school. Douglass would gladly name them, he says, in gratitude, but prudence forbids it, since to be named might embarrass them.

Sometimes, when the lessons were over, Frederick would tell the boys that they would be free as soon as they were twenty-one, while he himself would be a slave for life. Then he would ask them whether he did not have as good a right to be free as they did. The words troubled the boys, and they answered with kind sympathy and the hope that something would happen to set him free.

Douglass lived in Hugh Auld's family for about seven years, and during that time, despite the rules and the watchful eyes around him, he succeeded in learning both to read and to write. Nothing in the law helped him, and everything in it opposed him, so every letter he learned was a small victory. He did it, as he often says, in the odd minutes that nobody else could use.

When he was about twelve years old, Frederick got hold of a book called The Columbian Orator, a schoolbook full of speeches, poems and dialogues meant to teach young people the art of speaking well. Every spare moment he could steal, he spent reading it, and it was to become one of the most important books of his life. Nothing in it was written for a boy in his position, yet it spoke to him as if it had been.

One piece in the book was a dialogue between a master and a slave who had run away three times, and who was brought before him after being caught again. The master put forward all the usual arguments in defence of slavery, and the slave answered each of them so cleverly that, in the end, he was set free. Frederick read it again and again, delighted to find that his own half-formed thoughts could be said aloud, and well.

The book also contained the speeches of Sheridan, a great orator who argued in favour of giving equal rights to Catholics. Frederick read them over and over with unfailing interest, because they gave a voice to thoughts of his own that had often flashed through his mind and then died away for want of words. From the dialogue he took another lesson, which was that truth can have power over the conscience even of a slaveholder.

The more Frederick read, the more he came to abhor and detest his enslavers, and the more clearly he saw the wrong that was being done to him. His reading had opened his eyes to the truth about his position, but it had shown him no way of escaping from it. Knowledge, he found, could be a torment when it arrived without the power to act.

At times he felt that learning to read had been a curse rather than a blessing, for it had given him a clear view of his wretched condition without giving him the remedy. He envied his fellow slaves their ignorance, and in his darkest hours he wished that he were a beast, which would at least not know what it had lost. The thought of freedom, he says, haunted him like a ghost that would not leave.

Frederick kept hearing a strange word, abolition, always spoken by white men and usually with anger. When a slave ran away, set fire to a barn or attacked a master, the word was sure to be used, as if some hidden force were to blame. He could tell from their voices that it was important to him, but nobody would explain it.

At last he looked the word up in a dictionary, where he found that it meant the act of abolishing, and that explained very little. What was it, he wondered, that so many people were so anxious to abolish, and who were they? He did not dare to ask anyone, since he was sure that it was something that those around him wished him to know very little about.

One day a newspaper fell into his hands, and it told of petitions from the north asking Congress to end slavery in the District of Columbia and to stop the slave trade between the states. From that time on, he understood the words abolition and abolitionist, and he always drew near whenever they were spoken, hoping to hear something that mattered to himself and his fellow slaves. The light, he says, broke in upon him by degrees, and he began to see where his hopes might lie.

One day, while helping to unload a boatload of stone on a Baltimore dock, Frederick fell into conversation with two Irish workmen, who asked him whether he was a slave for life. When he said that he was, they seemed deeply moved, and they told him that it was a pity that such a fine young fellow should be a slave. They said that he ought to run away to the north, where he would find friends and be free.

Frederick, however, pretended that he was not affected by their words, for he had heard of men who tried to trap enslaved boys into confessing that they wanted to run away, in order to collect a reward. He hid his feelings and went on with his work, but the words stuck fast in his memory. The thought of the north, and of the friends who might be waiting there, never left him again.

From that day, the idea of escape took root in his mind, and he resolved to learn to write so that, when the time came, he could write a pass of his own. A slave travelling alone needed written permission from his master, and without it he could be stopped by any white man he met. Writing, like reading, was to be one more tool for his freedom, and one that nobody could take away.

In the shipyard where he sometimes worked, Frederick noticed that the carpenters marked each piece of timber with a letter, to show where it belonged on the ship. A letter for the left side, another for the right, another for the front and another for the back: he learned them all and began to copy them. Soon he was using the letters to spell out words, and the planks of the shipyard became his school.

Whenever Frederick met a boy who could write, he would say that he could write as well as the boy could. The boy would answer that he did not believe it and challenge him to prove it, and Frederick would chalk the letters he knew on a fence, only to be shown a few new ones in return. In this way, with a challenge here and a lesson there, he gathered most of what he knew about writing from the walls, fences and pavements of the city.

Tommy Auld, the small boy whom Frederick had once minded, went to school and filled several copybooks with his neat lessons, which were then put away in the house. When the family was out, Frederick would take them out, lay them open on the table and write in the spaces beneath the boy's lines, copying every stroke and curve. He practised until his handwriting began to match the schoolboy's, and nobody in the house suspected.

Captain Anthony died some years after Frederick had left the estate, leaving only a son, Andrew, and a daughter, Lucretia, to share his property. Everything he owned had to be valued so that it could be divided between them. Frederick was sent for at once from Baltimore, because he was part of that property.

Old and young, married and single, were counted in one list with the horses, the cattle and the pigs, and all were looked over in the same way. A grandmother with silver hair and a lively boy were weighed up with exactly the same eye, each given a price like any animal in the yard. Douglass never forgot the sight, and he describes it so that his readers will not forget it either.

Frederick dreaded most of all that he might be given to Andrew Anthony, who was known as a hard man and cruel to the people he owned. In the division, to his great relief, he fell to Lucretia, who had always been kind to him. He was released from the worst fear that a young slave on that estate could have.

In the division Frederick fell to Lucretia, who sent him straight back to Baltimore and to the Aulds. He returned gladly, feeling that he was going home to the only city and the only books he knew. His relief was great, though it was soon to be spoiled by what he learned of those he had left behind.

His grandmother, Betsy Bailey, had by now grown very old, and her owners no longer had any use for her. After a lifetime of service to the family, she was sent to live alone in a small hut in the woods, built with a mud chimney, and left there to manage as best she could. It was a house, Douglass says, in which an old woman was left to wait for death.

She had spent her life in the service of the Anthony family, and she had nursed their children and even their grandchildren, yet nobody cared for her when her own strength failed. Her sons and daughters, her grandchildren and the rest of her family had been scattered by sale and by hire to places she could not reach. In the darkness of her little hut she sat alone by a dying fire, with no hand to comfort her.

Douglass breaks off his plain account to ask a stern question, whether a righteous God will not punish a country for such deeds. The old woman had given her whole life to her masters and received, in return, a lonely hut and a lonely old age. In her fate he sees the truth that slavery rewards even the most faithful servant with nothing, and he asks his readers to feel it as he does.

Within a short time Lucretia died, and her brother Andrew soon followed her, so that the family that had owned Frederick was swept away. Their property was divided again among strangers, and Thomas Auld, Lucretia's husband, took another wife, Rowena Hamilton. Frederick, who was away in Baltimore, was spared the sight of it, though he felt the loss of the one kind mistress he had known on the plantation.

Some time later, a quarrel broke out between Thomas Auld and his brother Hugh, and in the heat of it Thomas decided to take Frederick away from Baltimore. Whatever the dispute was, the boy had no say in it, for a slave was a piece of property to be moved wherever his owner chose. He was sent to live with Thomas in the little town of St Michaels, on the other side of the Chesapeake.

In March 1832 Frederick left Baltimore, the city where he had learned to read and where he had first heard of abolition, and set out for St Michaels. He left behind the Aulds, the boys who had been his teachers and the books he loved, and he did not know whether he would ever see any of them again. Ahead of him lay the hardest and most dangerous years of his whole life as a slave.

At St Michaels Frederick soon found that Thomas Auld was a mean master, one who did not give the people he owned enough to eat. Among slaveholders themselves, Douglass notes, such meanness was thought a disgrace, for a good master was expected to feed his people well even if he worked them hard. After the better table of the Aulds in Baltimore, the change was a hard one to bear.

At St Michaels Frederick was often so hungry that he was driven to take food in secret from his master's supplies, and he did not feel that he was doing wrong. Douglass later explained his reasons carefully, because he knew that readers might judge him harshly. His account shows how hunger could make a clever boy think about justice and ownership.

Douglass argues that taking food from his master could not rightly be called stealing, because he and the food were both his master's property. By eating, he was only keeping that property alive and able to work, and moving it from one place to another did not change who owned it. It was a clever argument, but he makes it with a serious purpose, to show how slavery twists even the meaning of honesty.

In August 1832 Thomas Auld attended a Methodist camp meeting held by the bay in Talbot County, and returned announcing that he had experienced religion. Frederick allowed himself a faint hope that this conversion might lead his master to free his slaves, or at least make him kinder and more humane. The hope did not last long, as the weeks and months that followed soon showed him.

Instead of improving, Thomas Auld seemed to grow harder, and Douglass believes that he was a better man before his conversion than after it. He prayed morning and evening, held family prayers and filled his house with visiting preachers, yet his cruelty only increased. Religion, in his hands, had become a new reason to feel certain that he was right.

Douglass recalls that he saw his master tie up a lame young woman and whip her, and that Auld justified the act by quoting the Bible. The verse he chose was the one saying that a servant who knows his master's will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes. It showed Frederick how easily a sacred text could be turned into a weapon.

From what he saw at St Michaels and elsewhere, Douglass came to the sad conclusion that, of all the slaveholders he had known, the religious ones were the worst. They were often the meanest and most cowardly as well as the most cruel, because their religion gave them a cloak for their conduct and a kind of holy permission. Their churches, he adds, were full of men who prayed in the morning and bought and sold human beings in the afternoon.

Though his own master discouraged learning, Frederick began a Sunday school at St Michaels, where he taught other enslaved people to read the Bible. They came eagerly, and for a short time he knew the joy of passing on what he had worked so hard to gain. Douglass remembers the little school as one bright place in a dark and difficult year of his life.

The little school was soon discovered, and on one Sunday a band of white men, some of them members of the church, arrived with sticks and other weapons and drove the pupils out. They did not hide the reason, which was that an enslaved person who could read was a danger to the whole system. Douglass notes the bitter irony that men who professed to love the Bible had broken up a class that was learning to read it.

Thomas Auld declared that Frederick had been spoiled by life in the city and had become unmanageable, though the boy's only fault was that he had learned to think. At the end of that year he decided to hire him out for twelve months to a poor farmer named Edward Covey, who was famous in the district for breaking the spirit of young slaves. Douglass was about to enter the darkest and most dangerous period of his whole enslaved life.

Edward Covey was a poor man who rented his farm, and he had won a reputation across the district as a first-rate hand at breaking young slaves. He was also a member of the Methodist church and a class leader, a man who prayed aloud and loudly while treating the people under him with utter harshness. Owners with troublesome workers were glad to send them to him for a year.

On the first day of January 1833, Frederick set out on foot for Covey's farm, which lay about seven miles from St Michaels. He had been warned of what to expect, and he went with a heavy heart, carrying nothing but what he stood up in. It was the beginning of the hardest year of his enslaved life, and he knew it.

In his first week, Covey sent Frederick into the woods with a team of unbroken oxen, though the boy had never driven oxen in his life. The frightened animals bolted, wrecked the cart against a gate and nearly killed him, and Covey, instead of showing any concern, whipped him severely. It was only the first of the many whippings that Frederick was to receive during that long year.

Covey drove his workers from the first approach of day until its last lingering ray had left them, in every kind of weather and often beyond what human strength could bear. They were fed enough, but they were given hardly time to eat it, and he regarded rest as a theft from his own pocket. For the first six months, Frederick says, scarcely a week passed without a whipping.

Covey had a habit of creeping through the fields on his hands and knees, hidden by the tall corn, so as to spy on his workers, and the slaves nicknamed him the snake. He would suddenly rise to his feet a short distance from them and cry out, and nobody could ever be certain that he was not near. The result was that they worked in constant fear, whether he was watching or not.

Under Covey's rule, Frederick says, he was broken in body, soul and spirit, and he scarcely knew himself. His natural cheerfulness was crushed, his mind grew dull, the desire to read left him, and the spark that had once lit his eyes went out. It was, he writes, as though a man had been transformed into a brute.

Sundays were his only rest, and Frederick would stand alone on the high bank of Chesapeake Bay, watching the white sails of the ships pass in the distance. To free men they were a delight, but to him they were like shrouded ghosts, reminding him of all he had lost. He often stayed there for hours together, with a saddened heart and tearful eyes, until the light began to fade.

Frederick would speak aloud to the ships, as though they could hear him, telling them that they were loosed from their moorings and free while he was fast in his chains and a slave. They moved merrily before the gentle breeze, he said, while he moved sadly before the bloody whip, and he cried out that he wished he were on one of their decks. His words rose into the empty air, and the only answer was the wind.

At last, after a long and painful struggle with himself, Frederick made a firm and lasting resolve. He had only one life to lose, he told himself, and he would rather be killed while running than die slowly where he stood. About a hundred miles to the north, he reflected, lay a place where he might be free, and he promised himself that, with God's help, he would try for it.

Covey took great care to be seen as a man of religion, and he led his household in long and loud prayers every morning and evening. Yet Douglass never saw the slightest sign that his piety made him kinder to the people who laboured for him, and he came to see the prayers and the whippings as parts of the same system. The man who thanked God for his blessings at dawn would be driving his workers to exhaustion before the sun was high.

It was one of the hottest days of August 1833, and Frederick was working with three other men, fanning wheat in the yard. Hour after hour he laboured under the burning sun, until at last a violent headache and a wave of dizziness came over him and his strength began to fail. He knew that the signs were serious, but he also knew that Covey would not care.

At last Frederick sank to the ground, too weak to stand and too dizzy to see clearly. Covey, who was nearby, hurried over and kicked him in the side, ordering him to get up, but the young man could not obey. Then the farmer lost his temper completely and struck him on the head with a heavy piece of wood, and the blood ran freely.

Frederick decided that he must go to his master, Thomas Auld, and ask for protection, and he set out on the seven-mile journey to St Michaels. He staggered through the woods, his hair and clothes stiff with blood, afraid that Covey would catch him and that he himself would fall before he arrived. It was a bold step for a slave, since appeals of this kind seldom succeeded.

Thomas Auld at first seemed a little moved by the sight of his bleeding slave, but his mood soon changed. He said that Covey was a good man, that he could not think of taking Frederick away from him, and that, if he did, he would lose the whole year's wages. He told him to stay the night but to be back with Covey in the morning, or he would deal with him himself.

Obeying his master, Frederick returned to Covey's farm, where he arrived on Saturday morning, and Covey, who had been waiting for him, came out at once with a cowskin whip in his hand. Frederick turned and ran, plunging into the cornfield and then into the woods, where he lay hidden while the angry farmer searched in vain. He was now, in the eyes of the law, a runaway, hunted by a man who wanted him back.

He lay hidden in the woods for the rest of the day, hungry, sore and quite unsure what to do. If he went back to Covey, he was certain to be beaten, and if he stayed away, he would be hunted like an animal. It was a position from which there seemed no escape, and the long afternoon dragged on.

In the course of his wanderings Frederick met Sandy Jenkins, an enslaved man who was on his way to visit his wife, who was free and lived a few miles from Covey's farm. Sandy did not turn him away, though helping a runaway slave was a dangerous thing to do. He took him home, fed him and listened with sympathy to the story of what he had suffered.

Sandy advised Frederick to go back to Covey, and he gave him a certain root to carry in his right pocket, promising that as long as Frederick kept it there, no white man could whip him. Sandy swore that he had carried such a root for years and had never been struck since. Frederick thought the idea foolish, but to please the kind man who had helped him he agreed to take the root and keep it with him.

On Sunday morning Frederick walked back to the farm, and on the way he met Covey, dressed for church and apparently in the best of tempers. The farmer greeted him pleasantly and sent him to his work as if nothing had happened, so that Frederick wondered whether the root had really done its work. He did not believe that it had, but the change in the man was strange enough to make him doubt his own doubt.

On Monday morning, while Frederick was busy among the horses in the stable, Covey slipped in quietly with a rope in his hand. Before the young man understood what was happening, the farmer had seized him by the legs, meaning to tie him up and whip him as he had so often done. It was the moment, as it turned out, that was to decide everything that followed.

At that moment something rose up in Frederick that he could not explain, and he resolved to fight. He seized Covey by the throat and held him fast, while the astonished farmer clung to him in return, and the two men stood locked together in the stable. Douglass says that he did not know where the spirit came from, only that it had come.

Frederick's resistance was so entirely unexpected that Covey seemed to be taken aback, and Douglass says that he trembled in every limb like a leaf. The farmer asked whether the young man meant to go on resisting, and Frederick, with a steadiness that astonished himself, replied that he did, come what might. Both of them knew in that instant that the old order between them was broken for good.

Covey, alarmed, called for help, and a man named Hughes came to his aid, but when he tried to tie Frederick's hands, he received a kick that sent him staggering away. Covey then called on Bill Smith, a hired worker, who refused, saying that he had been hired to work and not to help whip anyone. Bill went about his business, and the two combatants were left to fight their own battle out.

The struggle went on for nearly two hours, until at last Covey, puffing and blowing, let Frederick go. He said, with what dignity he could muster, that he would not have whipped Frederick half so much if he had not resisted. The truth, Douglass observes with quiet humour, was that Covey had not whipped him at all, and had come off the worse in the contest.

For the remaining six months that Frederick spent with Covey, the farmer never again laid a hand on him in anger. Douglass suspects that the reason was vanity, for Covey could have had him publicly whipped, but that would have shown the whole district that a mere boy had beaten the famous slave breaker. His reputation as a breaker of slaves was worth more to him than any revenge.

The battle with Covey, Douglass writes, was the turning point in his career as a slave. It brought the last glowing coals of his hope back to life and gave him again a feeling of his own manhood, and it restored the self-confidence that months of cruelty had destroyed. He had been nothing before, he says, but now he was a man, and he meant to remain one.

From that day Frederick resolved that, however long he might remain a slave in form, the day had passed forever when he could be one in fact. He let it be understood, by his manner as much as by his words, that any white man who hoped to whip him would have to be prepared for a fight to the end. It was a stern vow, made by a young man who had discovered the one thing that the system could not take from him.

He describes the feeling that followed as a glorious resurrection, a rising from the tomb of slavery towards the heaven of freedom. His long-crushed spirit lifted, his cowardice fell away, and a bold defiance took its place. Only someone who has been whipped without resisting, he adds, can fully understand how such treatment destroys a person's pride.

Frederick stayed on Covey's farm until Christmas, when his year of hire came to an end. The work was as hard as ever, but the whippings had stopped, and he no longer went about with his head down. When the day came to leave, he did so with the sense of having won the only victory that was open to him.

Whether Sandy's root had any power, Frederick could never be sure, though he suspected it had none. What he knew with certainty was that his own decision to stand up and fight had altered his position, and that no charm in his pocket had done it. Hope, courage and a sudden act of defiance had done together what a year of obedience could never do.

Between Christmas and New Year, the enslaved were given a holiday of about six days, apart from the care of the animals. Those whose families lived far away were allowed to visit them, and the rest spent the days in ball games, wrestling, foot races, fiddling and dancing. Douglass remembers these days as the only time in the year when they seemed to belong to themselves.

Most of them spent the holiday in drinking whiskey, and this was the pastime that their masters liked best. A slave who chose to work through the holiday, or who refused to drink, was scorned as a lazy fellow who hardly deserved to be called a man. Some masters even encouraged the drinking with bets, to see which of them could swallow the most.

Douglass is convinced that the whole custom was a trick of the masters, designed to disgust the enslaved with the very idea of liberty. After days of drinking they would stagger back to work, sick and ashamed, and ready to believe that a free life was nothing better than this misery. The holidays, he says, worked like a safety valve, letting out the dangerous pressure that might otherwise have burst into revolt.

On the first of January 1834, Frederick began a new year on the farm of William Freeland, a man very different from Covey. Freeland was a well-bred southern gentleman with no pretence of religion, and for that reason Douglass found him a better master than any of the pious ones. He gave his workers enough to eat and time to eat it, and he treated them with a rough fairness.

On and around Freeland's farm Frederick found a circle of friends among the enslaved men, including Henry Harris, John Harris and the faithful Sandy Jenkins. They worked together, talked together and shared whatever food and news they had, and Frederick felt that he was among people who understood him. Their companionship would soon lead to a plan, and the plan to a great risk for all of them.

Frederick had not lost his passion for teaching, and at Freeland's he started a Sunday school once more, gathering friends from the surrounding farms in secret to learn to read. They met on Sundays, often out of sight, and on winter evenings by whatever light they could find. Every pupil knew that being discovered would mean a whipping, yet they came, because they wanted to read more than they feared the whip.

His pupils could pay him nothing and risked punishment for coming, yet they arrived with an eagerness that moved him deeply. He taught them what he knew, a letter and a word at a time, from a battered spelling book and the Bible. In their faces he saw proof that the hunger for knowledge was not limited to any race or condition.

Douglass says that he loved these friends with a love stronger than any he had felt since, for they were noble souls with hearts that were brave as well as loving. In a world that offered them little to be proud of, they shared what they had, trusted one another and kept every secret. It was among them, he believed, that he learned the true meaning of friendship.

Freeland was a fairer master than any Frederick had known, but the better treatment only sharpened his sense of what he was missing. A slave who is well fed and rarely beaten, he found, is still a slave, owned and priced like an animal and unable to choose his own road. The wish for freedom, which had never left him, now grew stronger and clearer with every passing week.

Frederick began to speak quietly to his pupils and friends about the possibility of escape, and he found that they felt as he did. After many whispered conversations, they agreed that they would make a bid for freedom together, and they began to think hard about how it might be done. It was a dangerous secret, and every one of them knew that the smallest slip might cost them everything.

As the plan took shape, Frederick and his friends tried to face the dangers honestly and in full. They might be caught and beaten, they might be thrown into jail, and worst of all they might be sold to a trader and carried far away to the South, never to see their families again. After many nights of whispered argument, they agreed unanimously that they would rather face all of it than spend the rest of their lives as slaves.

Their plan was to take a large canoe belonging to William Hamilton on the Saturday night before the Easter holidays and to paddle up Chesapeake Bay for about seventy miles. At the head of the bay they would turn the canoe adrift and follow the North Star on foot until they had passed beyond the limits of Maryland. Everything depended on speed, on secrecy and on the faithful guidance of a single distant star.

They had chosen the water route for a sound reason, which was that they would be less likely to be taken for runaways. A group of men paddling a canoe might be mistaken for fishermen, whereas on the roads they would have been questioned and stopped at every turn. Frederick had thought through each detail with great care, as a man does when his life depends on it.

To make the journey look innocent, Frederick wrote a pass for each of the men, stating that the bearer had full liberty from his master to spend the Easter holidays in Baltimore. He signed each one with the name of William Hamilton, a farmer who lived near St Michaels, in the hope that no one who met them would think to question it. It was a skill that he owed to the copybooks and the chalk, and now it might be turned to a greater purpose.

As the great day approached, the friends grew more anxious, though they did their best to look as they always did. Freedom or death, they told one another, was now their resolve, and they promised to stand by each other whatever happened. Frederick knew that he had led them into a great risk, and the thought of it weighed heavily on him.

On the morning they were to leave, Frederick went to work as usual, but he was overcome by a strong feeling that something was wrong. He told his friends that he believed they had been betrayed, though he could not have said how he knew. Even so, nothing could be done except to go on as if nothing were wrong and to wait for evening.

Soon afterwards, William Hamilton rode up to the farm in great haste, followed by two constables and several other men, some of them armed. They went straight for Frederick and his friends, seized them and tied their wrists with rope, while the astonished workers watched. When the young men asked the reason, they were told that they were accused of planning to run away.

As the ropes were tied, Frederick whispered to his friends the one rule that might save them, which was to own nothing and to deny everything. In the confusion, each of them quietly got rid of the pass he carried, so that the men who searched them found no written proof. It was a small act of cunning, and it was to make the difference between a whipping and something far worse.

At St Michaels the young men were questioned before a group of angry white men, and each of them denied that there had ever been a plan to escape. Without the passes, there was no proof, and the accusers had only the word of whoever had betrayed them. Their calm denials held firm, and the men who questioned them could find nothing to prove.

The prisoners were marched, tied together, to the county jail at Easton, the chief town of Talbot County. Frederick, whom the authorities seemed to regard as the ringleader, expected the worst, for in that part of Maryland a slave who had planned to run away was often sold to a trader and sent far away. As the cell door closed behind them, the dream of freedom seemed further away than ever.

One by one, his friends were released and taken home by their masters, until Frederick alone remained in the cell. He had no illusions about what that might mean, for the authorities believed that he had led the others, and a slave who was thought to be a leader could expect little mercy. The days that followed left him alone with his thoughts, his fears and his memories of his friends.

To his great surprise, Frederick was not sold to a trader, as he had feared. Thomas Auld came to the jail and took him out, and after some consideration he decided to send him back to Baltimore, to live once more with his brother Hugh and to learn a trade. Douglass does not pretend to know all of Auld's reasons, but he knew that the road to the South had been closed, at least for now.

Frederick returned to the city that he had loved as a boy, and Hugh and Sophia Auld received him back into their house. The place seemed familiar and strange at once, for he was no longer a child, and in his heart he carried the memory of a failed attempt and the determination to try again. The city, with its crowded streets and its harbour full of ships, offered him far better chances of escape than the countryside ever had.

Hugh Auld hired Frederick out to Mr Gardner, a shipbuilder, who was racing to complete two large warships for the Mexican government. Frederick was sent to help the carpenters and to learn the trade, but in the rush he was ordered about by a dozen men at once. Fetch this, hold that, bring water, move the timber: from morning until night the commands came from every side.

The white carpenters in the yard feared that Black workmen would lower their wages, and they said openly that these men were taking the bread out of their mouths. First they drove out the free Black carpenters, and then, with the same resentment, they turned on Frederick, who was a slave and could not complain. Douglass sees in their anger a bitter example of how poor men were taught to blame one another.

One day four or five of the white apprentices attacked Frederick together, striking him with their fists, a brick and a heavy handspike. He fought back as well as he could, but the numbers were against him, and his left eye was so badly injured that it was feared he might lose it. Around them, a crowd of white workmen watched, and some of them shouted that he ought to be killed.

Frederick staggered home to the Aulds' house in Fell's Point, his face swollen and covered with blood. Sophia, who had grown so cold towards him, was moved to tears at the sight, and for a while her old kindness returned as she dressed his wounds with her own hands. Hugh Auld was furious too, and it seemed, for one afternoon, that the household had remembered what it had once been.

Hugh Auld took Frederick to Esquire Watson, a magistrate, to demand a warrant against the boys who had attacked him. Watson listened and then explained that, since the law would not accept the evidence of a Black man against a white one, he could do nothing unless a white person would swear to what had happened. Many white carpenters had seen it all, yet not one would come forward, and the attackers went free.

Hugh Auld refused to send Frederick back to Gardner's yard and moved him to another, run by Walter Price. There he learned caulking, which means driving tarred fibre into the seams of a ship's hull to keep the sea out, and he proved so quick at it that he soon earned a skilled workman's wage. It was a trade that Douglass was to make use of sooner than anyone could have guessed.

Frederick earned as much as six or seven dollars in a week, and every Saturday evening he had to hand all of it to Hugh Auld. Hugh would sometimes give him back a few cents to encourage him, and the gesture had the opposite effect, since it showed him plainly whose money it was. He felt that he was being robbed of the money that he had earned by his own labour.

In the spring of 1838, Frederick asked his owners for the privilege of hiring his own time, which meant finding his own work and paying his master a fixed sum each week. Thomas Auld refused at once, but Hugh Auld, who saw a profit in it, consented on strict terms. Frederick was to pay him three dollars every Saturday night and to provide his own tools, food and clothing, whether he found work or not.

It was a hard bargain, for Frederick owed Hugh the three dollars whether or not he found employment, and he had to furnish his own tools, food and clothing out of whatever was left. Even so, he greatly preferred the new arrangement to the old, because it gave him some control over his own hours and a modest share of what he earned. He tasted something of what it might mean to be free, and he was determined not to lose it.

In August 1838, Frederick went to a religious camp meeting outside the city, and when he returned, he was a little late with his weekly payment. Hugh Auld flew into a rage, scolded him bitterly, and declared that Frederick should not be allowed to hire his own time in future. The anger was out of all proportion to the offence, and it told Frederick exactly how his master saw him.

Frederick had made up his mind that the time had come, and the anger of Hugh Auld only hardened his resolve. He returned to work as usual, said nothing to anyone, and gave no sign of what he meant to do, for a single careless word could have cost him everything. Behind his steady face a plan was already taking shape, as clear and cold as a winter morning.

On the third of September 1838, Frederick left his chains behind him, and he succeeded, as he says, in reaching New York without the slightest interruption of any kind. The journey from slavery to freedom, which had cost him years of planning and the failure of one great attempt, was over in a very short time. He was about twenty years old, and for the first time in his life he was entirely free.

Douglass refuses to describe how he escaped, and he explains his reasons with care. To publish the details, he says, would help slaveholders to close the roads that others might use, and it might bring danger and ruin to the friends who had helped him. He even criticises the habit of some abolitionists of speaking so openly about their secret routes that the underground railroad was becoming something more like an upperground one.

When he reached New York, Frederick felt like a man who had escaped from a den of hungry lions, and the joy of it was like nothing he had ever known. He was free, with no master to whip him, to hire him out or to sell him, and no one could take from him the wages of his own work. The feeling, however, did not last long, for another one soon crept in beside it.

Soon the first joy gave way to a deep sense of loneliness and fear. Frederick was free, but he was a stranger in a great city, without home, friends, money or credit, and he dared not speak to anyone for fear of choosing the wrong person. Kidnappers who hunted fugitives for the reward, he knew, were common in the city, and the North, which he had imagined as a promised land, felt for the moment like a trap.

At last a kindly sailor noticed the young man's trouble and asked him quietly whether he was a fugitive. Frederick, who had been afraid to trust anyone, took a chance on the stranger's honest face and told him the truth. The sailor took him home and promised to find him a friend who would know what to do.

The sailor brought Frederick to David Ruggles, a Black abolitionist who spent his days helping fugitives in New York. Ruggles welcomed the exhausted young man warmly, gave him a bed and a meal, and asked nothing in return except the truth. After a day of fear and years of waiting, Frederick had at last found a place where he could rest without looking over his shoulder.

Safe in Ruggles's house, Frederick wrote to Anna Murray, a free woman of Baltimore whom he hoped to marry, and asked her to come to New York. She came, and their reunion was one of the happiest moments of his life. From that day she shared every step of his new life, through its hardships as well as its triumphs.

A few days after Anna arrived, she and Frederick were married by the Reverend James Pennington, a Black minister who was himself a fugitive from slavery. Ruggles gave them a certificate of marriage and a Bible, and the little ceremony was a quiet one. For the first time in his life, Frederick could call a family his own, with no master able to part them.

Ruggles feared that New York was too dangerous for a fugitive, with slave catchers and kidnappers at large in its streets, so he advised the couple to travel to New Bedford, in Massachusetts. There, he said, the shipyards needed caulkers, and the people were friendly to men like Frederick. They left almost at once, with very little money but a great deal of hope.

In New Bedford the couple were taken to the house of Nathan Johnson, a Black man who received them with warm hospitality and provided for all their needs. He and his wife took a deep and lively interest in their welfare, and Douglass says that they proved themselves entirely worthy of the name of abolitionists. After so much fear and so many hardships, it was a gentle and generous landing into a new country.

Frederick had already changed his name once, dropping the surname Bailey and calling himself Frederick Johnson, in order to avoid being traced by those who hunted fugitives. In New Bedford, however, there were so many Johnsons that it was hard to tell one from another, and he found that he must change again. He asked his host to choose a name for him, with one condition, that he must keep Frederick, which he wished to hold on to as a sign of his own identity.

Nathan Johnson had been reading The Lady of the Lake, the famous poem by Sir Walter Scott, and he suggested the name Douglass, after one of its noble Scottish heroes. Frederick liked the sound of it, and he took it as his own, though he insisted on keeping the name Frederick. From that day to the end of his life, he was known to the world as Frederick Douglass.

He had half expected that a country without slaves would be poor and wretched, and he was astonished by what he saw in New Bedford. The harbour was crowded with ships, the wharves were piled with goods, and the working people lived in neat and comfortable houses, better than those of many slaveholders in Maryland. Everything was done by free hands, and the town prospered, which was for him a revelation.

Frederick took whatever honest work he could find, and in New Bedford that meant common labour of every kind. He sawed wood, shovelled coal, dug cellars, swept chimneys and rolled heavy oil casks along the wharves, and he did it all with pleasure, because every cent of his wages belonged to him alone. For the first time he understood what it meant to work for himself and to keep what he earned.

Soon after he settled in New Bedford, Frederick began to take The Liberator, the antislavery newspaper edited by William Lloyd Garrison, and he read every issue with hungry eagerness. Its sympathy for the enslaved, its fierce attacks on slaveholders and its truthful exposures of slavery set his soul on fire, and the paper became his meat and drink. He could hardly have guessed that the man who edited it would one day write the preface to his own book.

In August 1841 Frederick attended an antislavery convention on the island of Nantucket, where he was unexpectedly urged to speak. He felt a deep reluctance, for slavery had taught him to doubt his own abilities, but he rose and told his story, and found his tongue loosed as soon as he began. William Lloyd Garrison followed him with a speech of his own, and the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society soon asked the young fugitive to become one of its agents.

After finishing the story of his life, Douglass reread it and noticed that, in several places, he had spoken so sharply about religion that readers might take him for an enemy of all faith. To remove that danger, he added a short appendix in which he explained what he meant and what he did not mean. It is one of the most carefully argued parts of the book, and it shows that he regarded the matter as seriously as anything he had written.

Douglass says that he sees the widest possible difference between the Christianity of this land and the Christianity of Christ, so wide that a person must choose between them. I love the pure, peaceable and impartial religion of Christ, he declares, and for that very reason I hate the hypocritical religion that blesses slaveholding. He regards the second as one of the boldest frauds ever practised, and he will not allow it to borrow the name that Christ made holy.

He accuses the churches of the slaveholding states of sharing in the very wrong they should have condemned, for there were ministers who bought and sold human beings and missionaries who whipped women. Such men prayed in public, raised money for churches and sent Bibles overseas, while they tore families apart at home. He closes with a bitter parody of a hymn, whose verses mock pious preachers who whip their slaves and then sing of heavenly union, and he leaves it without comment.

Douglass closes his book with a pledge, saying that he sincerely hopes his little work may throw light on the American slave system and hasten the glad day of deliverance for the millions of his brethren in bonds. He relies, he says, on the power of truth, love and justice, and he promises himself anew to the sacred cause. He signs it simply with his name, dating it from Lynn, Massachusetts, in April 1845, and the book is finished.

The Narrative was an immediate success, selling thousands of copies within months and winning readers across the United States and beyond. Yet its fame was also a danger, for the book named Douglass's former owners and made it plain that he was a fugitive, and his friends feared that he might be seized and sent back into slavery. In the late summer of 1845 he sailed for Britain, where he could speak in safety.

Douglass spent almost two years in Britain and Ireland, speaking in churches and halls to audiences who had never heard a man tell of slavery from his own experience. An edition of his Narrative was printed in Dublin, and more were issued in Britain, so that his words travelled farther than he could have dreamed. Everywhere he went, he found people who were willing to listen and to help.

While he was abroad, a group of British friends, among them Ellen Richardson, raised money to buy Douglass's freedom and paid about 150 pounds to Hugh Auld. Some abolitionists complained that paying a slaveholder only confirmed his claim to own a human being, but Douglass accepted the gift with gratitude. When he returned to America in 1847, he came home as a legally free man, safe at last from the fear of being seized and sent back.

In December 1847 he began his own newspaper, The North Star, in Rochester, New York, so that Black Americans would have a voice that was not edited by anyone else. A few months later he attended the first women's rights convention at Seneca Falls and spoke in favour of giving women the vote, though many of his friends thought the idea too bold. He believed all his life that the cause of freedom could not be divided.

When the Civil War came, Douglass pressed President Abraham Lincoln to make the destruction of slavery a purpose of the war and to allow Black men to serve as soldiers. He helped to recruit them himself, and two of his own sons joined the army, while he met the President at the White House more than once. Their conversations, Douglass later said, left him with a deep respect for the President, who treated him as an equal.

Frederick Douglass died in Washington on 20 February 1895, after a long career as an editor, a speaker, a writer and a servant of his country. His Narrative remains one of the great works of American literature, read in schools and homes around the world and admired for its clarity, its courage and its dignity. It shows that a person who has learned to read and to think can never be wholly enslaved, and that freedom begins, long before the law grants it, in the mind.
